archetypes.title: Agent-facing endpoint
summary: A service built to be called by other organisations' agents rather than by their engineers — including agent-initiated commerce. The caller is autonomous, acting for a human who is not present, and every assumption about who is on the other end has to be restated.
description:
Bot defence and agent enablement point in opposite directions, and this archetype is the decision about which way to face. A decade of investment went into distinguishing humans from automation and blocking the automation; an agent acting for a legitimate customer trips every one of those signals. Continuing to block treats customers as attackers, and simply allowing removes the defences that stop actual abuse. The resolution is a distinct, authenticated, rate-limited path for agents rather than a hole in the human one.
Delegation is the substance of it. The question is not whether the caller is a bot but whether this agent is authorised to act for this customer, to what extent, and for how long. That demands a delegation model with real primitives — an agent identity, a scope, an expiry and a revocation path — and none of it works retroactively on an API designed for humans with sessions.
Where the endpoint takes payment, the emerging rails add mandates: a signed statement of what the human authorised, presented by the agent and verifiable by the merchant. That is the right shape and it is new, competing and unsettled, so the durable position is to build the mandate check as its own component rather than couple to one scheme.
The remaining differences from a human-facing API are all about behaviour. Agents retry, so idempotency is a correctness requirement rather than a nicety. Agents parallelise, so limits tuned for human pacing do not hold. Agents read error messages and act on them, so error text is part of the interface in a way it never was. And a dispute over an agent's action needs a record of the mandate it presented, not only of the request it sent.
distinguishedBy:
Against a remote MCP server: that publishes tools for agents to call. This publishes a business API, and the caller may be any agent framework at all. The MCP archetype's descriptions-as- prompt problem does not arise; the delegation and payment questions dominate instead.
Against an ordinary API with bot management: same endpoint, opposite policy. That one is trying to identify and block automation. This one is trying to admit it under a delegation model, which is a different system rather than a relaxed setting.

exemplars.name: Agent-accessible commerce endpoints
exemplars.note: Merchants exposing a path for agent-initiated purchasing, with a mandate presented by the agent and verified before the transaction.

exemplars.name: Agent payment and mandate rails
exemplars.note: Competing specifications for expressing what a human authorised an agent to spend, backed by card networks, platforms and standards bodies. Unsettled, and worth abstracting behind a component of your own.

exemplars.name: Business APIs adding an agent lane
exemplars.note: An existing API gaining a separate authenticated path for agent callers, with its own limits and its own audit, rather than loosening the human one.

zones.note: Third-party agents, the humans they act for, and the platforms whose delegation claims the endpoint has to evaluate.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Where agent traffic is separated from human traffic and admitted on its own terms.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: Mandate verification, business logic, and the idempotency that makes retries safe.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: Orders, accounts and the evidence trail a disputed agent action will be argued from.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: Agent registration, delegation policy, limits and dispute evidence.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Third-party agent
nodes.note: Someone else's agent, running on someone else's infrastructure, acting for a customer. Not a bot to be blocked and not a user to be trusted.

nodes.label: Delegating customer
nodes.note: The person on whose behalf the agent acts, absent at request time. Their authorisation has to arrive as a verifiable artifact rather than as an assertion.

nodes.label: Agent lane
nodes.note: A separate authenticated path with its own limits and its own audit. Separation is what lets bot defences stay strict on the human path.

nodes.label: Agent authentication
nodes.note: Establishes which agent, from which operator, acting for which customer. Three facts, and most API authentication was built to establish one.

nodes.label: Agent rate limits
nodes.note: Tuned for callers that retry and parallelise. Limits derived from human pacing do not survive contact with an agent.

nodes.label: Mandate verification
nodes.note: Validates the signed statement of what the human authorised — scope, value, expiry. Built as its own component because the schemes competing to define it are unsettled.

nodes.label: Idempotency and reconciliation
nodes.note: Agents retry on timeouts and ambiguity. Without idempotency keys, a retried purchase is a second purchase, and the customer's agent did it.

nodes.label: Transaction processing
nodes.note: The actual operation, bounded by whatever the mandate turned out to permit.

nodes.label: Response and error text
nodes.note: Agents read errors and act on them, so error text is now part of the interface. Verbose failures teach an agent to retry differently, and teach an attacker the same thing.

nodes.label: Orders and accounts
nodes.note: The state the transaction changes, and what a dispute will be resolved against.

nodes.label: Mandate evidence
nodes.note: The mandate presented, the agent that presented it and the action taken. A disputed agent transaction is unarguable without it.

nodes.label: Agent registry
nodes.note: Which agent operators are recognised and what each may do. Turns an unbounded population of callers into an administered one.

nodes.label: Delegation policy
nodes.note: What an agent may do for a customer without further confirmation, and above what threshold the human has to be reached on another channel.

nodes.label: Dispute and reversal
nodes.note: What happens when a customer says their agent was not authorised to do that. Needs to exist before the first one, and rests entirely on the evidence trail.

nodes.label: Agent behaviour monitoring
nodes.note: Baselines per agent operator rather than per user, because normal for an agent is nothing like normal for a person and the old baselines flag all of it.

control.note: Happens entirely outside this system, on a platform the merchant does not operate. All the endpoint ever sees is the artifact that results.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Two separate claims: which agent this is, and what its human authorised. Conflating them — treating a recognised agent as an authorised one — is the central failure of this archetype.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Establishes the operator, which is the party accountable when an agent misbehaves at scale.
control.title: Agent identity

control.note: Agent, operator and customer travel with the request rather than being re-derived from its body — which an agent composes.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Scoped to the mandate rather than the request, so a retry with a fresh request id does not become a second transaction.
control.title: Replay safety

control.note: Bounded by what the human authorised rather than by what the agent asked for. The mandate is the authorisation; the request is just a request.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Retained as long as a dispute can be raised, because reconstructing what an absent human authorised is otherwise impossible.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: Read by a model and acted on. Error text is now interface design, and a verbose failure teaches the caller — and anyone probing — more than it should.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: An unregistered agent gets the human path and its bot defences, which is the correct default rather than an outage.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: Above the threshold the human is reached on another channel; below it the mandate suffices. Where the line sits is the archetype's central business decision.
control.title: Per-invocation policy

control.note: Per operator rather than per user. Human baselines flag every agent, which is why the old detection cannot simply be pointed at this lane.
control.title: Independent discovery

control.note: The entire dispute rests on the mandate evidence. A record of the request without the mandate cannot establish whether the agent exceeded its authority.
control.title: Append-only audit

crossCutting.note: The archetype in one risk. A recognised agent is not an authorised one, and the human who could clarify is not there. Every control here exists to keep those two facts separate.
The caller population is unbounded and lives outside the organisation. Registration converts it into something administered; without it, admitting agents means admitting anyone.
An agent acting beyond its mandate, or the same action executing twice on a retry. Mandate scope and idempotency address different halves and neither covers both.

deviations.subject: No model appears in this architecture
deviations.reason: Like the remote MCP server, this service contains no AI. It is in the catalogue because its caller is one, and because a decade of bot defence assumed the opposite. Everything distinctive here follows from the caller's nature.

deviations.subject: Mandate verification is drawn as input handling
deviations.reason: It is an authorization decision and would sit more naturally in the control plane. It is drawn inline because it has to happen per request, before the transaction, and because treating it as policy configuration rather than a request-path component is how it ends up being skipped on the retry path.

deviations.subject: The mandate is drawn without naming a scheme
deviations.reason: Several competing specifications exist and none has settled. Drawing one would date the diagram and imply a coupling that is not advisable yet; the component is drawn and the schemes are named only in the exemplars, which carry dates.

archetypes.title: AI-augmented API backend
summary: A conventional API with a model somewhere in the middle — classifying, extracting, summarising or routing — behind a contract that promises a typed response. The most widespread AI architecture and the least often recognised as one.
description:
There is no chat interface here and frequently no user-visible AI at all. A support ticket gets categorised, an invoice gets extracted, a message gets routed, a document gets summarised, and the caller receives a normal API response. The AI is an implementation detail of an endpoint, which is exactly why this archetype tends to skip the controls the chat-shaped ones get.
The defining property is that model output re-enters a deterministic system. Downstream code branches on a classification, writes an extracted value to a record, or passes a generated string into a query. The model's output is untrusted input to everything after it, and the single most valuable control is schema validation with a deterministic failure path — a response that does not conform is rejected rather than coerced.
Free-text fields inside a structured response are where this goes wrong. A schema that validates shape but leaves a string field unconstrained has validated nothing about the content of that field, and that string is often the one that reaches a template, a query or another prompt. Constraining to enumerations wherever the domain allows is worth more than any filter.
Two operational properties differ from a normal backend and catch teams out. Latency and availability now depend on an external inference call, so timeouts, retries and a deterministic fallback path are functional requirements rather than resilience niceties. And cost is per-token on a path that may be called at request volume, which makes an unbounded input a financial exposure as well as a performance one.
distinguishedBy:
Against the embedded retrieval assistant: no conversation, no retrieval, no human reading the output. The consumer of the model's output is code, which changes the control set from grounding and rendering to schema validation and fallback.
Against an autonomous action agent: this has no loop and no discretion. It performs one transformation per request within a fixed contract. Where the extracted value drives a write, the write is the calling system's decision, not the model's.
Against a batch pipeline: same transformation, synchronous and in the request path, so latency and availability become the caller's problem rather than a schedule's.

exemplars.name: Classification and routing endpoints
exemplars.note: Ticket triage, content moderation, intent routing. A typed response consumed by code, with the model replacing a rules engine that used to be maintained by hand.

exemplars.name: Document extraction services
exemplars.note: Invoices, forms and contracts turned into structured records. The extracted values are written to systems of record, which is where the validation question becomes concrete.

zones.note: Callers, and the documents and text they submit for processing.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: The published contract, and the quotas and authentication in front of it.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: The transformation, the validation, and the deterministic path taken when the model does not cooperate.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: Where extracted values and classifications land.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: The published inference interface.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Credentials, quotas, evaluation and the record of what the model was asked and answered.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Calling system
nodes.note: Another service or a customer integration. Expects a typed response and will not tolerate a prose apology when the model misbehaves.

nodes.label: Submitted content
nodes.note: Ticket text, uploaded documents, message bodies. Written by whoever submitted them, and reaching a prompt without ever looking like a prompt to the developer who wrote the endpoint.

nodes.label: API endpoint
nodes.note: The published contract. Its promise of a typed response is what the whole validation discipline downstream exists to keep.

nodes.label: Input validation
nodes.note: Size, type and content limits before anything reaches a model. On a per-token dependency, bounding input length is a cost control as much as a safety one.

nodes.label: Transformation
nodes.note: Builds the prompt, calls the model, and is the only place in the service that knows an AI is involved at all.

nodes.label: Output validation
nodes.note: Schema conformance with rejection rather than coercion, then constraints on the fields themselves — enumerations where the domain allows, encoding for wherever a free-text value is about to land. Validating shape alone says nothing about the contents of a string.

nodes.label: Deterministic fallback
nodes.note: What the endpoint returns when the model is slow, unavailable or non-conforming. A functional requirement, because the contract promised a response.

nodes.label: Record write
nodes.note: Where an extracted value or a classification becomes state. The caller's decision to trust the output, made concrete.

nodes.label: Inference API
nodes.note: The published interface, and now part of this endpoint's latency and availability budget.

nodes.label: Credential broker
nodes.note: Short-lived provider credentials rather than a key in the service's configuration.

nodes.label: Accuracy and adversarial evaluation
nodes.note: Behaviour on a labelled set, and on inputs designed to break the schema. Where a chat product degrades noticeably, this one silently miscategorises.

nodes.label: Quota and cost ceiling
nodes.note: A per-token dependency called at request volume. Without a ceiling, traffic and cost are the same variable.

nodes.label: Prompt and response log
nodes.note: What was sent and what came back, per request. The only way to reconstruct why a record holds the value it does.

control.note: Conventional API authentication. Authenticates the caller and nothing about the content they submitted, which is the part that reaches the model.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Submitted content is bounded and classified before it becomes a prompt. Easily skipped here, because the endpoint does not look like an AI feature to whoever wrote it.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: The edge has already bounded size and stripped what it can. Everything after this point treats the payload as adversarial regardless.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Issued per workload rather than held in the service's configuration.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Authenticated transport carrying unauthenticated content into a deterministic system. Every control from here to the write path exists because of this crossing.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: What crosses back out is a validated, constrained object rather than model text. That is the contract the endpoint published, and the only thing that keeps it true.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: The same contract, honoured without the model. A caller cannot tell the difference, which is the property that makes the dependency survivable.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: The model influenced the value; it did not authorise the write. Keeping those separate is what stops this archetype from quietly becoming an action agent.
control.title: Per-invocation policy

control.note: Issued at call time to a workload that proved what it is. Nothing in the service tier holds a provider key at rest.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Enforced at the edge, because by the service tier the token spend is already committed.
control.title: Quota and rate limit

control.note: Tests that the schema holds under adversarial input, not only that accuracy is acceptable on the happy path.
control.title: Evaluation gate

control.note: The only record of why a field holds the value it does. Frequently omitted here precisely because the endpoint does not look like an AI feature.
control.title: Append-only audit

crossCutting.note: The archetype's central risk. Model output flows into branching logic, record writes and sometimes queries, and every consumer of it was written expecting a value rather than an adversary.
Arrives inside ordinary business content, on an endpoint nobody thinks of as an AI feature. That framing is what causes the injection controls to be skipped here more than anywhere else.
An external inference call sits inside a synchronous request path. Latency, availability and cost become the caller's problem, which is why the fallback path is functional rather than defensive.

deviations.subject: The calling system is drawn as a third-party agent rather than a user
deviations.reason: It is usually another service, sometimes an agent, and only occasionally a person. The third-party-agent type carries the property that matters — a non-human caller with its own credential and its own retry behaviour — which is what shapes the quota and idempotency requirements.

deviations.subject: A deterministic fallback is drawn as a routing node
deviations.reason: It is not a security control and would not normally appear on a security diagram. It is drawn because the alternative to it is returning model output that failed validation, which is precisely the failure the schema check exists to prevent.

deviations.subject: No retrieval appears
deviations.reason: Many real implementations add it. It is left out to keep this archetype distinct from the retrieval assistant — the transformation-behind-a-contract shape is what is being described, and adding retrieval makes it that other archetype with a typed response.

archetypes.title: AI gateway, router and guardrail plane
summary: A shared platform service every AI workload calls through: routing across models and providers, quotas, guardrails, redaction and one complete log. The chokepoint an organisation builds once so the other archetypes do not each solve the same problems differently.
description:
This archetype exists because of a counting argument. Twenty teams calling model providers directly produce twenty credential stores, twenty logging conventions, twenty quota decisions and no aggregate view. One gateway produces one of each. Nothing about it is novel infrastructure — it is an egress proxy specialised for a metered, non-deterministic dependency — and its value is entirely in being the only path.
Which makes network enforcement the load-bearing control. A gateway that teams are asked to use is a convention, and conventions lose to deadlines. Default-deny egress to model endpoints with the gateway as the sole exception is what converts it into an architecture. Everything else on this diagram assumes that enforcement holds.
The gateway is also the highest-value target in an organisation's AI estate. Every prompt and every response passes through it, which means it sees more sensitive data than any single application, and it holds the provider credentials for all of them. Its own access control, its own log retention and its own blast radius deserve the treatment given to a secrets manager, not the treatment given to a proxy.
Two design cautions. Guardrails at the gateway see text without application context, so they catch policy violations and generic injection patterns and cannot judge whether a particular retrieval was appropriate — application-level controls remain necessary, and the gateway is a backstop rather than a replacement. And a semantic cache that returns one caller's response to another is a disclosure path wearing a performance feature's clothes.
distinguishedBy:
Against managed model API consumption: that archetype is about the relationship with one provider. This is about operating the crossing as a platform for many teams and several providers, with the failover, cost attribution and policy uniformity that implies.
Against the internal AI platform: that is the whole paved road, including agent runtimes and data plumbing. This is one component of it, and usually the first one built because it is the one that pays for itself immediately.

exemplars.name: Managed AI gateways
exemplars.note: Cloud and CDN-operated gateways offering routing, caching, quotas and observability across multiple model providers behind one endpoint.

exemplars.name: Self-operated proxy layers
exemplars.note: An open-source or in-house proxy standardising on one API shape across providers, with per-team keys, budgets and logging.

zones.note: The model providers, and content that arrives in prompts from elsewhere.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Every AI workload in the organisation. The population this exists to serve.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: The single crossing. Its value is proportional to how completely it is the only one, and its sensitivity is proportional to how much passes through it.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: Policy, credentials, budgets, the model catalogue and the aggregate view.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Model providers
nodes.note: Several, deliberately. Multi-provider routing is a resilience property and a negotiating position, and it is only practical if something normalises them.

nodes.label: Content inside prompts
nodes.note: Whatever the workloads put in context. The gateway sees the text and not the application logic that assembled it, which bounds what its guardrails can conclude.

nodes.label: AI workloads
nodes.note: Applications, agents and pipelines. Whether they can reach a provider without passing through the gateway decides whether this archetype is real.

nodes.label: Gateway endpoint
nodes.note: One API shape across providers, which is what makes routing and failover possible without changing every caller.

nodes.label: Prompt redaction
nodes.note: Detecting and masking sensitive values on the way out. The last chance to stop a secret or a personal identifier reaching a provider, applied uniformly rather than per team.

nodes.label: Guardrail enforcement
nodes.note: Content and injection classification, inbound and outbound. Uniform policy without application context, which makes it a backstop rather than the primary defence.

nodes.label: Model routing and failover
nodes.note: Selects a provider by capability, cost or availability, and fails over when one degrades. Turns a hard provider dependency into a soft one.

nodes.label: Response cache
nodes.note: Reuses responses across similar requests to cut cost and latency. Keyed loosely enough to cross tenants, it returns one caller's data to another — a disclosure path dressed as a performance feature.

nodes.label: Provider egress
nodes.note: The actual crossing, holding the provider credentials so no workload has to. Also the reason this tier is the organisation's highest-value AI target.

nodes.label: Egress enforcement
nodes.note: Default-deny to model endpoints, gateway excepted. Without it the gateway is a suggestion, and every other control here rests on it.

nodes.label: Provider credentials
nodes.note: All of them, in one place, rotatable in one operation. Concentration is the benefit and the exposure at the same time.

nodes.label: Budgets and quotas
nodes.note: Per team, per workload, per model. Also the cost attribution finance asks for, which is frequently what funds the gateway in the first place.

nodes.label: Model catalogue
nodes.note: Which models are approved, pinned and deprecated. One place to roll a provider version change rather than a coordinated migration across every caller.

nodes.label: Aggregate observability
nodes.note: Every prompt, response, model, caller and cost. The most sensitive log in the estate, and the only complete one.

control.note: Per caller rather than a shared gateway key, because quota, attribution and the log all key off it. A shared key makes the aggregate view anonymous.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Uniform classification for every workload. The gateway sees text without application context, so this is a floor beneath the application's own controls rather than a replacement for them.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: The scoping is the control. A key that ignores the caller returns one tenant's response to another, and it will look like a cache hit rather than an incident.
control.title: Memory scoping

control.note: The credential never leaves this tier. One rotation point for the organisation, and the reason a compromise of this tier is a compromise of every provider relationship at once.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: The return leg passes through the guardrail too. Output-side policy is the half most often omitted, and the half that catches a model that has been successfully steered.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Context-correct output handling still belongs to the caller, because only it knows where the text is about to be rendered or executed.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: The control everything else depends on. A gateway teams are asked to use is a convention; a gateway that is the only reachable path is an architecture.
control.title: Egress allowlist

control.note: One store, one rotation, and no provider key anywhere in an application's configuration.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Inline rather than reported after the fact. A monthly cost report is not a control on an agent that can loop.
control.title: Quota and rate limit

control.note: Pinning here means one place to test and roll a provider version change, instead of coordinating a migration across every caller.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: Complete because there is one crossing, and therefore the most sensitive log in the estate. It needs the access control and retention limits of a secrets store, not of a proxy log.
control.title: Append-only audit

crossCutting.note: The gateway's entire value is being the only path, and that is a network property rather than an application one. Every control on this diagram is conditional on the egress policy holding.
Concentration cuts both ways. One place to redact, one place to log and one place to rotate — and one place that sees every prompt in the organisation and holds every provider credential.
Caller identity has to survive from the workload through routing, caching and logging. A shared key or a loosely-keyed cache collapses the separation at a different point each time.

deviations.subject: Model providers are drawn in the outside world rather than in a vendor zone
deviations.reason: Every other archetype gives the provider a vendorOpaque zone. Here there are several and the archetype's subject is the crossing rather than any one relationship, so they are drawn as external endpoints. The single-provider relationship is the managed model API archetype.

deviations.subject: The guardrail is drawn once but sits on both legs
deviations.reason: Inbound and outbound policy are usually the same service, and drawing it twice would suggest two components. Both edges route through it, and the return leg is called out because it is the one most often left unimplemented.

deviations.subject: The response cache is drawn although many deployments do not run one
deviations.reason: It is optional and it is the component most likely to be enabled for cost reasons without a review. Drawing it gives the cross-tenant keying question a place to be asked.

archetypes.title: Text-to-SQL analytics agent
summary: A natural-language interface over a data warehouse that generates and runs queries against live records. The semantic layer is the security control, and treating it as a modelling convenience is the characteristic mistake.
description:
This is the one archetype where the model composes executable code against production data as its normal mode of operation. Retrieval assistants read a pre-built index; this one writes a query and runs it. That makes the question not "what was indexed" but "what can be expressed", and expressiveness is exactly what a query language is for.
Filtering generated SQL is not a viable control. A language rich enough to be useful is rich enough to evade a filter, and the history of SQL injection defence is a long argument for constraining what can be constructed rather than inspecting what was. The semantic layer is that constraint: a curated set of tables, columns, joins and metrics the generator may reference, with row-level policy attached. Anything outside it cannot be named, so it cannot be queried.
The second control is the execution identity. The query must run as the asking user, not as a service account with warehouse-wide read. Where the warehouse supports row-level security and column masking, running as the user makes those policies apply automatically and turns the entire access-control question into one the data platform already answers. A service account turns every generated query into a potential entitlement bypass.
Aggregation is the risk with no clean technical answer. A user entitled to see aggregates can often reconstruct individuals by asking enough narrow questions, and each individual query is legitimate. Query logging and pattern detection over a session is the realistic control, and it is detective rather than preventive.
Cost and blast radius are the operational pair. A generated query can scan a warehouse, and a generated write would be unrecoverable — which is why the execution role should be read-only and the cost ceiling should be per query rather than per month.
distinguishedBy:
Against the embedded retrieval assistant: that one retrieves from an index built earlier; this one composes a query against live data. The control moves from index-time permissions to the semantic layer and the execution identity.
Against the AI-augmented API backend: both produce structured output consumed by code, but here the output is executed rather than validated and stored. Schema validation does not help when the schema is "a valid query".

exemplars.name: Warehouse-native analytics agents
exemplars.note: Natural-language querying built into a data platform, executing against a curated semantic model with the platform's own row-level security applied.

exemplars.name: BI assistant layers
exemplars.note: Conversational front ends over an existing BI semantic model, which is the best case: the constraint layer already exists and was built for a different reason.

zones.note: The analyst asking, and content that reached the warehouse from elsewhere.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Where the question becomes a query, and where the query is constrained before it runs.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: The semantic layer, the execution engine and the records. Most of this archetype's security is the data platform's existing machinery, used properly.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: The published inference interface.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Semantic-layer curation, entitlements, query audit and aggregation monitoring.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Analyst
nodes.note: Asks in natural language. Their entitlements should be the whole of what the answer can contain, which is only true if the query runs as them.

nodes.label: Content in the warehouse
nodes.note: Free-text columns holding customer and partner input. Returned in results and summarised back into context, which makes the warehouse an injection path.

nodes.label: Question interface
nodes.note: The conversational surface, and the session the queries are attributed to.

nodes.label: Query generation
nodes.note: Turns the question into a query, given the semantic layer's description of what exists. Composes executable code against production data as its normal operation.

nodes.label: Query constraint check
nodes.note: Confirms the generated query references only the semantic layer, is read-only, and is bounded. A safety net over the constraint, not a filter on SQL — filtering a query language is a game the filter loses.

nodes.label: Result summarisation
nodes.note: Turns rows back into prose. Row content re-enters the model here, which is the injection path that starts in a customer-entered field and ends in an analyst's answer.

nodes.label: Semantic layer
nodes.note: The curated tables, joins, metrics and row policies the generator may reference. This is the security control of the archetype: what cannot be named cannot be queried.

nodes.label: Query execution
nodes.note: Runs the query as the asking user, so the platform's row-level security and column masking apply without the application re-implementing them.

nodes.label: Warehouse records
nodes.note: Live production data, including everything outside the semantic layer that should stay unnameable.

nodes.label: Inference API
nodes.note: Receives the schema description and the question, and later the result rows for summarisation. Both directions carry data worth accounting for.

nodes.label: Semantic layer curation
nodes.note: Deciding what is exposed and what stays out. A security review disguised as a data-modelling task, and usually staffed as the latter.

nodes.label: Identity and entitlements
nodes.note: Carries the analyst's identity through to execution. Whether it survives that far is the difference between an access-control system that holds and one this archetype bypasses.

nodes.label: Query and aggregation monitoring
nodes.note: Watching sequences of individually legitimate queries that together reconstruct individuals. Detective, because there is no preventive answer to this at query granularity.

nodes.label: Query cost ceiling
nodes.note: Per-query scan and runtime limits. A generated query can scan the warehouse, and the person who asked did not know they were asking for that.

control.note: The identity established here has to reach the execution engine intact. Everything about this archetype's access control depends on that one property.
control.title: User identity

control.note: The generator is shown only what it may use. Describing the full warehouse to the model and hoping it behaves is the failure mode this control exists to prevent.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: Sends the curated schema and the question. The schema is a description of the business, which is itself worth accounting for in data-handling terms.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Executable code arriving from an unauthenticated content channel. This is the crossing that makes the constraint check non-negotiable.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Executed as the asking user rather than a service account, so row-level security and column masking apply. A service account here turns every query into an entitlement bypass.
control.title: User identity

control.note: The data platform's own enforcement, applied because the query arrived with a real user identity. Reusing it is worth more than anything the application could build.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: Customer-entered text lands in columns that will be returned and summarised. The injection arrives through data collection, not through the assistant.
control.title: Existing content permissions

control.note: The rows that come back are already filtered by row-level security. What crosses here is exactly what the analyst was entitled to see — and it is about to be sent to a provider.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: The return leg sends actual records to the provider. Frequently overlooked when accounting for what this archetype discloses.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Adding a table here is granting access to it. Treating semantic-model changes as data modelling rather than as authorisation is the characteristic mistake of this archetype.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: The single most important control on the diagram. If the identity is swapped for a service account anywhere along the path, every other control here is decorative.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Per session, because the aggregation risk lives in the sequence rather than in any single query. Logging queries individually and never reading them together misses it entirely.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: Enforced by the platform, because by the time the query is running the cost is committed.
control.title: Quota and rate limit

crossCutting.note: A sequence of legitimate aggregate queries reconstructing individuals. No single query is wrong and no node can prevent it, which is why the only realistic control is detective and operates over a session rather than a request.
Three paths: what the query returns, what the schema description reveals about the business, and what the result rows disclose when sent for summarisation. Only the first is usually accounted for.
The user's identity has to survive from the question to the execution engine. Every hop is an opportunity to substitute a service account, and one substitution voids the entire model.

deviations.subject: The execution engine uses the actuator node type
deviations.reason: It reads rather than writes, and actuator normally marks a write path. It is used because the security-relevant property is the same: this is where the model's output stops being text and starts having an effect, and where the identity it runs under decides the blast radius.

deviations.subject: No query-filtering node appears
deviations.reason: Filtering generated SQL is the control teams reach for first and it does not hold — a language expressive enough to be useful is expressive enough to evade inspection. The constraint check that is drawn verifies the query stays inside the semantic layer, which is a different and tractable question.

deviations.subject: Most of the security machinery is attributed to the data platform
deviations.reason: Row-level security, column masking and resource governance already exist and were built for other reasons. Drawing them as application controls would suggest reimplementing them, which is both expensive and worse.

archetypes.title: Batch and offline AI pipeline
summary: Scheduled, high-volume model inference over stored data — enriching records, classifying a backlog, generating embeddings, summarising a corpus. Nobody is watching, and the output becomes durable state that later systems treat as fact.
description:
The distinguishing property is that the output persists and loses its provenance. A synchronous endpoint's mistake affects one response; a batch job's mistake is written into a million records that downstream systems, analysts and other models will read as ground truth for years. By the time anyone notices, the derived data has been copied into three other places.
This makes provenance the primary control rather than a compliance nicety. Every generated field wants to carry which model version produced it, when, from what source and at what confidence — because the only realistic response to a discovered defect is to find and regenerate the affected subset, and that is impossible without the stamp.
Poisoning scales here in a way it does not elsewhere. Content that reaches a batch job affects everything the job produces, and where the output feeds a retrieval index or a training set, one poisoned input has been amplified across a corpus and made durable. Sampling and drift detection on output distributions catch this; per-record validation generally does not, because each individual record looks fine.
Operationally the risks are the mundane ones with unusual severity. Volume plus per-token pricing makes an unbounded job a financial event. Retries without idempotency duplicate both cost and output. And a pipeline that fails halfway leaves a corpus in a state where some records have the new treatment and some do not, which is worse for downstream consumers than either outcome alone.
distinguishedBy:
Against the AI-augmented API backend: the same transformation on a schedule instead of in a request. Latency stops mattering and durability starts: nobody is waiting, and the output will outlive the job by years.
Against the fine-tuning pipeline: that one produces a model, this one produces data. They share the build-system trust properties, and the artifact and its blast radius are different.
Against the retrieval assistant's ingest half: closely related, and this archetype generalises it. Ingest is a batch pipeline whose output happens to be an index.

exemplars.name: Bulk enrichment and classification
exemplars.note: Scheduled jobs adding derived fields to a warehouse — sentiment, category, extracted entities — consumed thereafter by analysts and other systems as though they were collected data.

exemplars.name: Embedding generation at corpus scale
exemplars.note: Re-embedding a corpus on a schedule or after a model change. The output is an index, and the job's failure modes are the index's failure modes.

exemplars.name: Provider batch inference tiers
exemplars.note: Discounted asynchronous inference for large volumes, which makes this archetype cheap enough to run over everything and therefore common.

zones.note: Where the source data was authored, by parties the pipeline never authenticates.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Orchestration, batching and the transformation. Runs on a schedule under a service identity with no human in the loop.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: The source corpus and the derived output, which downstream systems cannot tell apart.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: Inference, often on a discounted asynchronous tier.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Provenance, sampling, budget and the ability to find and undo what a bad run produced.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Source content authors
nodes.note: Whoever wrote the records being processed — customers, partners, staff, other systems. One hostile input is amplified across everything the job produces.

nodes.label: Schedule
nodes.note: Starts the run with nobody watching. There is no user to notice that the output looks wrong, which is why sampling replaces observation here.

nodes.label: Job orchestration
nodes.note: Batching, checkpointing, retries and idempotency. Retry without idempotency duplicates both the output and the bill.

nodes.label: Prompt construction
nodes.note: Turns each record into a prompt. Source content and instruction are concatenated here, at volume, with no review of any individual result.

nodes.label: Output validation
nodes.note: Schema conformance and range checks per record. Catches malformed output and not systematic drift, because each bad record looks individually plausible.

nodes.label: Provenance stamping
nodes.note: Model version, run identifier, timestamp, source record and confidence on every generated field. Without it, a defect discovered later cannot be scoped, and regeneration is a full re-run of everything.

nodes.label: Source corpus
nodes.note: The records being processed, and the permissions the derived output should inherit.

nodes.label: Derived data
nodes.note: Generated fields, embeddings and summaries. Downstream systems read these as facts, and nothing about their shape says a model produced them.

nodes.label: Batch inference
nodes.note: Asynchronous, discounted, and holding a large volume of the corpus for the duration of the job. Retention terms matter more here than on a per-request path.

nodes.label: Output sampling
nodes.note: Human and automated review of a sample per run, plus distribution comparison against the previous one. The only control that catches systematic error at this volume.

nodes.label: Run budget and ceiling
nodes.note: A hard stop on tokens and spend per run. Volume multiplied by per-token pricing with no ceiling is an open commitment, and the job has no user to abandon it.

nodes.label: Run and lineage registry
nodes.note: Which run produced which records with which model version. The artifact that makes a targeted rollback possible instead of a full regeneration.

nodes.label: Pipeline identity
nodes.note: A service identity with read access across the corpus and write access to the derived store. Broader than any user's, and unattended.

control.note: Nothing AI-specific gates this, and it happened long before the pipeline existed. One poisoned record becomes an influence on everything the run produces.
control.title: Existing content permissions

control.note: Broader than any individual's access, because the job processes everything. Whether the derived output inherits the source's permissions is decided downstream, and often not at all.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: Carries a large share of the corpus to the provider in one submission, which makes the retention terms on the batch tier a material question rather than boilerplate.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Unauthenticated content arriving at volume, with nobody reading it. Every downstream consumer will treat what survives validation as collected data.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Write access limited to the derived store rather than the source. A pipeline that can overwrite its own inputs makes the defect unrecoverable.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Comparing this run's output distribution against the last is what catches a model change or a poisoning campaign. Per-record validation cannot see either.
control.title: Evaluation gate

control.note: A hard stop rather than an alert, because there is no user watching to abandon a runaway job.
control.title: Quota and rate limit

control.note: The version recorded has to be the version used. Stamping a configured value rather than the one the provider actually served makes the lineage confidently wrong.
control.title: Verified provenance

control.note: Read on the source, write on the derived store, and nothing else. The asymmetry is what keeps a bad run recoverable.
control.title: Workload identity

crossCutting.note: Amplified and made durable. One hostile input influences an entire run's output, which is then read as fact by systems and people who never see the pipeline. Provenance and sampling are the only controls that scale to it.
Derived data is indistinguishable from collected data once written, so it flows into training sets and indexes downstream. Without the stamp nobody can tell what a model generated.
Volume, per-token pricing, retries and no human watching. Each is fine; together they are the most common way this archetype produces an incident that is purely financial.

deviations.subject: Derived data uses the index node type
deviations.reason: It is often a warehouse table rather than a vector index. The index type is used because the security-relevant property is the same: a second body of data with its own permissions and its own freshness, derived from a source whose access controls it may or may not carry.

deviations.subject: Provenance stamping is drawn as a pipeline node rather than a governance control
deviations.reason: It is a governance concern, but it has to happen inside the write path to be true. Drawing it in the control plane would suggest it could be applied afterwards, and a provenance stamp added later is a guess.

deviations.subject: No human appears anywhere except in sampling
deviations.reason: That is the archetype. The single human touchpoint is a sample of the output after the fact, and putting it in the control plane rather than the flow states plainly that nobody reviews the run itself.

archetypes.title: Multi-agent durable workflow
summary: Several agents collaborating on a long-running process, coordinated by a durable execution engine that journals every step so the work survives crashes. The journal is what makes it reliable, and it is also a secrets sink and a replay surface.
description:
Durable execution works by recording the result of every step and replaying the journal to rebuild state after a failure. That is an excellent reliability property and it has two security consequences nobody expects from a workflow engine. Everything a step returns is written down, so a step that returns a credential has persisted it. And the engine replays steps, so a step that is not idempotent can execute its side effect more than once — including an agent's tool call, and including a payment.
Delegation between agents is the second axis. A supervisor decomposing work for subagents is the common shape, and the trap is that the subagent inherits the supervisor's authority rather than a narrowed slice of it. Delegation that does not narrow is privilege distribution: a research subagent that can also issue refunds because its parent can. Each hop should carry less, and the chain should be reconstructable afterwards.
Inter-agent messages are model output becoming model input. One agent's result lands in another's context with the standing of an instruction, and a compromised or merely confused agent propagates through the graph. This is the failure mode that distinguishes multi-agent systems from a single agent with more tools: cascading, and hard to attribute after the fact because every message looks like a legitimate one.
Long duration adds two more. Credentials issued at the start may outlive their validity or their appropriateness by the time a step runs days later, which argues for fetching at step time rather than holding. And an unbounded loop between agents burns tokens for as long as nobody notices — which, on a process designed to run for days, can be a while.
distinguishedBy:
Against the autonomous action agent: that one decides and acts, usually within seconds. This one coordinates several agents over hours or days, and its distinctive risks — journal contents, replay, delegation depth, cascading — all come from duration and multiplicity rather than from the act itself.
Against the sandboxed execution service: that contains a compromise inside one task. This survives failure across many. A workflow may invoke a sandbox as a step; the concerns are orthogonal.

exemplars.name: Durable execution engines running agent steps
exemplars.note: Workflow platforms that journal step results and replay to recover, with agent invocations as steps alongside conventional ones.

exemplars.name: Supervisor and subagent orchestration
exemplars.note: A coordinating agent decomposing work across specialists, each with its own context and tool set, over a process too long to hold in one conversation.

zones.note: The initiator, and content the workflow reads from systems it does not control.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: The durable engine, the supervisor, and the journal that makes recovery possible.
zones.label: Compute tier · orchestration

zones.note: Subagents with their own contexts and tools, exchanging results as messages.
zones.label: Compute tier · agents

zones.note: The journal, the shared memory, and the systems the workflow actually changes.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: The published inference interface, called many times across the process.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Delegation policy, credentials, budget, audit and the ability to stop a running process.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Initiator
nodes.note: Starts the process and is absent for the rest of it. The approval they gave at the start is the only human decision until something escalates.

nodes.label: External content
nodes.note: Documents, records and API responses the workflow reads over its lifetime. Every one is a chance to steer an agent whose output another agent will trust.

nodes.label: Durable execution engine
nodes.note: Runs steps, records results, replays to recover. Reliability machinery whose recording and replay behaviours are both security-relevant.

nodes.label: Supervisor agent
nodes.note: Decomposes the goal and delegates. Holds the broadest authority in the system, which is why what it passes down matters more than what it holds.

nodes.label: Subagents
nodes.note: Specialists with their own contexts and tools. Each should hold a narrower authority than its parent; inheriting the parent's is delegation that escalates.

nodes.label: Inter-agent messages
nodes.note: One agent's output becoming another's instruction. The propagation path for a compromise, and the reason a multi-agent failure is hard to attribute afterwards.

nodes.label: Tool gateway
nodes.note: Scoped per agent rather than per workflow. Where the narrowing that delegation should perform is actually enforced.

nodes.label: Execution journal
nodes.note: Append-only record of every step's inputs and results, replayed to recover. Whatever a step returned is now durable, which makes a step that returns a secret a secret at rest.

nodes.label: Shared workflow memory
nodes.note: Cross-agent and cross-session by construction. A poisoned entry influences every agent that reads it, for the rest of the process.

nodes.label: External effects
nodes.note: The writes, payments and provisioning the workflow performs. Idempotency here is what makes replay safe, and replay is not optional in a durable engine.

nodes.label: Inference API
nodes.note: Called many times across the process, by several agents, over a long period.

nodes.label: Delegation policy
nodes.note: What a parent may pass to a child, and how deep the chain may go. Each hop narrowing is the property that keeps a subagent from inheriting the supervisor's reach.

nodes.label: Credential broker
nodes.note: Fetched at step time rather than held for the process. On a workflow that runs for days, a credential taken at the start is stale, over-scoped, or in the journal.

nodes.label: Loop and budget limits
nodes.note: Depth, iteration and token ceilings. A cycle between two agents on a process expected to run for days can burn a great deal before anyone looks.

nodes.label: Delegation trace
nodes.note: Which agent asked which, with what authority, and why. Without it a multi-agent failure is unattributable, because every message in the chain looked legitimate.

nodes.label: Workflow termination
nodes.note: Halting a process mid-flight and deciding what to do with its partial effects. Harder than in any other archetype here, because the effects are already partly applied.

control.note: The initiator's entitlements bound the whole process. Capturing them at the start is what stops a step running days later from exceeding what they could have done.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Each hop should carry less than the one above it. Passing the parent's authority unchanged is the most common defect in this archetype and it is invisible until something goes wrong.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: The sender is authenticated and what it says is not. A subagent's result arrives in the supervisor's context with the standing of a fact.
control.title: Agent identity

control.note: Content read mid-process is classified before it enters an agent's context, because that agent's output becomes another's instruction and the error propagates.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: At step time, not at workflow start. A token held across a multi-day process is either expired or over-scoped by the time it is used.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: The idempotency key is a security control here, not a reliability nicety: the engine will replay this step, and a non-idempotent effect executes twice.
control.title: Replay safety

control.note: Whatever a step returned is now durable and readable by anyone who can read the journal. A step that returns a secret has stored it, and replay will hand it back.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: Replay re-derives state without re-checking whether the original authorisation still holds. A step legitimate on Monday replays unchanged on Thursday.
control.title: Replay safety

control.note: Cross-agent by design, which is the point and the risk. A poisoned entry reaches every agent that reads it for the remainder of the process.
control.title: Memory scoping

control.note: At each hop rather than once at the start, because the chain is built dynamically and its depth is not known when the workflow begins.
control.title: Per-invocation policy

control.note: Fetching rather than holding is what keeps credentials out of the journal. A step that returns a secret has written it down permanently.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: A cycle between two agents is invisible for as long as the process was expected to run.
control.title: Quota and rate limit

control.note: Parent, child, authority passed and reason. The only way to answer which agent caused an outcome once several have contributed to it.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: Stopping is easy; deciding what to do with half-applied effects is not. The compensating path has to be designed with the workflow rather than discovered during an incident.
control.title: Emergency stop

crossCutting.note: One agent's output is another's input, so an error or an injection propagates through the graph and arrives looking like a legitimate result. This is the risk that distinguishes a multi-agent system from a single agent with more tools.
Authority flows down a chain built at runtime. Without a trace of who delegated what to whom, an outcome cannot be attributed to a decision, and the chain cannot be audited at all.
The journal records everything every step returned, permanently, to make recovery work. It is a reliability mechanism that is also a data store nobody designed as one.

deviations.subject: The execution journal is drawn as a memory store
deviations.reason: It is a reliability mechanism, not a memory feature, and its designers would not call it one. It is typed as memory because its security properties are memory's — durable, cross-session, re-read as context on replay — and typing it as infrastructure would hide that entirely.

deviations.subject: Replay is drawn as an edge running backwards from the journal
deviations.reason: No other diagram here has an edge that re-executes history. It is drawn because replay without re-authorisation is a genuine and underappreciated property of durable execution, and it has no other place to appear.

deviations.subject: Two of this archetype's risks have no CoSAI equivalent
deviations.reason: OWASP's agentic taxonomy names memory poisoning and cascading hallucination as distinct threats, and CoSAI's risk set has neither. They are mapped here to prompt injection and insecure model output, which are the nearest true statements but lose the compounding that makes both dangerous in a multi-agent system. Recorded rather than papered over, because the gap belongs to the source taxonomy and not to this diagram.

deviations.subject: Subagents are drawn as one node
deviations.reason: There are several, with different contexts and tools. They are drawn as one because the risks — inherited authority, message propagation, chain opacity — are properties of the delegation pattern rather than of any particular specialist.

archetypes.title: Internal multi-tenant AI platform
summary: The paved road: a shared platform on which product teams build AI features, with the gateway, the agent runtime, the data plumbing and the guardrails supplied centrally. The archetype whose unit of concern is the population of workloads rather than any one of them.
description:
Every organisation that gets past its third AI workload builds some version of this, usually after discovering it has three different credential arrangements and no aggregate view. The platform's purpose is to make the governed path the easy path, so that a team choosing the quickest route also chooses the controlled one.
That framing produces the archetype's design rule: adoption is a security control. A platform teams route around because it is slow, restrictive or badly documented produces worse outcomes than no platform, because it also produces the belief that AI use is governed. The measure of this architecture is what fraction of workloads actually run on it, and that number should be monitored as carefully as any control.
Tenancy is the hard technical part. Product teams share a gateway, a vector store, an agent runtime and a set of node pools, and the isolation between them is a platform property nobody on a product team can verify. Namespace, network and data isolation each fail differently, and a shared vector store with per-tenant filtering rather than per-tenant separation is a disclosure waiting for a query bug.
The platform's own access is the concentration risk. Platform operators can typically read across tenants by construction, the central log holds every product's prompts, and the shared credential store holds every provider relationship. The platform team's own privileges deserve the scrutiny normally reserved for a domain administrator, and they rarely get it.
Finally, this is where organisation-wide controls become possible at all. Model approval, evaluation gates, inventory and cost attribution work here and cannot work anywhere else, because there is nowhere else that sees all of it.
distinguishedBy:
Against the AI gateway: that is one component of this, and usually the first built. This is the whole paved road — runtime, data plane, templates and standards — with the population problem as its subject.
Against the vendor low-code agent builder: the same paved-road intent with the paving done in-house. Here the environment model, the deployment gate and the isolation are designed rather than selected, and the builders are engineers rather than business users.
Against any single application archetype: those describe one workload. This describes the substrate several of them share, and its risks are aggregation, isolation and adoption rather than anything in a request path.

exemplars.name: Internal AI platform teams
exemplars.note: A central team offering gateway, runtime, vector store and templates as a product to internal product teams, with an onboarding path and a support rota.

exemplars.name: Multi-tenant generative AI platform reference designs
exemplars.note: Cloud providers publish this as a named architecture, which is a reasonable indicator that most large organisations converge on it.

zones.note: Model providers, and the end users of whatever the product teams build.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: The tenants. Each builds its own workload, and each can leave the platform if it is easier to.
zones.label: Compute tier · tenant workloads

zones.note: Gateway, runtime and templates, shared across tenants. The isolation between tenants is a property of this tier that no tenant can verify.
zones.label: Compute tier · shared platform

zones.note: Vector stores, memory and feature data. Per-tenant separation or per-tenant filtering — a choice with very different failure modes.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: The organisation-wide controls that are only possible because there is one place that sees everything.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Model providers
nodes.note: Several, consumed on behalf of every tenant through one relationship each.

nodes.label: Product workloads
nodes.note: Whatever each team is building — an assistant, an agent, a pipeline. Each is one of the other archetypes in this catalogue, running here.

nodes.label: Onboarding path
nodes.note: How a team gets started. Its friction is a security parameter: a slow onboarding produces workloads that were built somewhere else.

nodes.label: Shared AI gateway
nodes.note: One crossing to model providers for every tenant, with per-tenant quotas, logging and cost attribution. Described in full as its own archetype.

nodes.label: Shared agent runtime
nodes.note: A common place to run agents, with sandboxing, identity and observability supplied. Tenants inherit controls they did not have to build.

nodes.label: Paved-road templates
nodes.note: Reference implementations with the controls already wired. The most effective security artifact the platform produces, and the one most often under-invested in.

nodes.label: Shared vector store
nodes.note: Several tenants' embeddings in one system. Per-tenant separation is a design decision; per-tenant filtering is one query bug away from cross-tenant disclosure.

nodes.label: Shared memory and state
nodes.note: Session and agent state across tenants. Keying is the whole of the isolation, and a key that omits the tenant collapses it silently.

nodes.label: Tenancy and isolation policy
nodes.note: Namespace, network and data isolation between tenants. A platform property no tenant can verify, which makes it the platform team's obligation to state and test.

nodes.label: Approved model catalogue
nodes.note: Which models any tenant may use, at which versions, with which terms. An organisation-wide control that only works because there is one gateway.

nodes.label: Workload inventory
nodes.note: Every AI workload, its owner, its data, its models and its risk classification. The artifact an auditor asks for and the one that does not exist without a platform.

nodes.label: Shared evaluation service
nodes.note: Adversarial and safety testing offered as a service, so each team does not build its own and most therefore actually do it.

nodes.label: Platform operator access
nodes.note: The platform team can typically read across every tenant by construction. Their privileges deserve domain-administrator scrutiny and rarely receive it.

nodes.label: Adoption and drift monitoring
nodes.note: What fraction of AI workloads actually run here, and which teams left. Treated as a product metric and functioning as a security one.

nodes.label: Central observability
nodes.note: Every prompt, tool call and cost across every tenant. The most sensitive log the organisation holds, and the only complete one.

control.note: Registration is how a workload enters the inventory. A team that starts without it is invisible to every governance control on this diagram.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: Controls arriving pre-wired. Also a supply chain into every workload, which makes template review a platform-wide security activity.
control.title: Artifact integrity

control.note: Per tenant, because quota, cost attribution and the log all key off it. A shared platform credential makes every downstream record anonymous.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Isolation asserted by the platform and unverifiable by the tenant, which is why the tenancy policy has to be stated and tested rather than assumed.
control.title: Isolation boundary

control.note: Separation means a bug returns nothing; filtering means a bug returns another tenant's data. The difference only shows up when something goes wrong.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: A key that omits the tenant collapses isolation silently and looks like a cache hit rather than a breach.
control.title: Memory scoping

control.note: One relationship per provider, used on behalf of every tenant. Concentration is the benefit and the exposure at once.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: The tenant cannot test it, so the platform has to — and has to publish the result, or the guarantee is just a claim in a wiki.
control.title: Isolation boundary

control.note: An organisation-wide model policy, enforceable only because there is one crossing. Without the gateway this control cannot exist at all.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: Both, because self-registration finds the compliant teams and discovery finds the rest.
control.title: Independent discovery

control.note: Central provision is why teams actually evaluate. A policy requiring evaluation without supplying a harness produces evidence rather than testing.
control.title: Evaluation gate

control.note: The platform team can read every tenant's prompts. That is the concentration risk of this archetype and it deserves the treatment given to domain administration.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: Tenant-tagged so a product team can see its own without seeing everyone's, which is the access-control question the central log poses.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: The platform's adoption rate is a security metric. Workloads that left are workloads with none of these controls, and the reason they left is usually fixable.
control.title: Independent discovery

crossCutting.note: Gateway, runtime, vector store and memory are all shared, and each isolates differently. Tenancy is not one component's property — it is a claim about four of them at once, and only the platform team can test it.
A platform teams route around is worse than none, because it also produces the belief that AI use is governed. Adoption is the control, and friction is the vulnerability.
Concentration. One log with every prompt, one credential store with every provider relationship, and one team that can read across all of it.

deviations.subject: This archetype contains other archetypes
deviations.reason: Its tenants are assistants, agents and pipelines already described elsewhere in this catalogue, so it overlaps all of them by construction. It is drawn because its risks — tenancy, concentration and adoption — belong to none of them individually and appear nowhere else. The product workloads are deliberately one node.

deviations.subject: Adoption monitoring is drawn as a security control
deviations.reason: It is a product metric and would not normally appear on a security diagram. It is drawn because every control here applies only to workloads that are on the platform, which makes the adoption rate the multiplier on all of them.

deviations.subject: Platform operator access is drawn as an identity node in the control plane
deviations.reason: It is a risk rather than a control, and the vocabulary has no node type for a privileged insider. It is placed here because the concentration of access is a defining property of the archetype and needs somewhere to be stated rather than left implicit.
