archetypes.title: Managed agent runtime
summary: A cloud provider's hosted agent service — the loop, the memory, the tool gateway, the sandbox and the identity all supplied as managed components. The governance plane arrives built in, and the trade is that it is configured rather than designed.
description:
Every provider converged on the same decomposition during 2026: a runtime, a memory service, a gateway for tools, an identity service, a code interpreter, a browser, observability, an evaluation service and a policy engine. That convergence is itself the finding — the governance plane the risk-map taxonomy has no components for is exactly what these services sell.
The consequential choice is between the managed harness and the code escape hatch. Every provider offers both: a declarative agent whose loop they run, and a bring-your-own-code runtime where they supply the sandbox and the identity but the loop is the customer's. The first inherits the platform's guardrails automatically; the second inherits only what it explicitly calls. Teams routinely start with the first, hit a limitation, move to the second, and do not notice which controls stopped applying.
Managed memory deserves specific attention because it is the component most likely to be switched on without a decision. Its scope — per session, per user, or shared across users — is a configuration flag with a data-protection consequence, and cross-user memory means one user's content can influence another's turn.
The genuine advantage is agent identity. These platforms issue agents first-class, revocable identities distinct from the service and from the user, which is the control most self-built agent architectures never get around to. Using it properly — rather than running everything as one service principal — is most of what separates a well-governed deployment from a poorly governed one on the same platform.
The costs are portability and opacity. The decomposition differs enough between providers that the agent, its memory model and its policy expressions do not move; and the loop's internals are not inspectable, so debugging a misbehaviour means reading traces rather than code.
distinguishedBy:
Against building the agent tier: the same components with the provider supplying them. The work moves from designing an identity model, a policy engine and a sandbox to configuring three, and from having to build observability to having to export it.
Against the vendor in-app action agent: that agent belongs to a SaaS product and acts on its records. This is a platform for building the customer's own agents on the customer's own data, with the loop hosted rather than the application.

exemplars.name: Hyperscaler agent runtimes
exemplars.note: Managed agent services decomposed into runtime, memory, gateway, identity, sandbox, observability, evaluation and policy, billed per component.

exemplars.name: Managed harness with a code escape hatch
exemplars.note: A declarative agent the provider runs, alongside a bring-your-own-code runtime for cases the declarative form cannot express. The pair is now standard across providers.

zones.note: Users, and the content agents read from systems the platform does not govern.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: The customer's own front end and the agent definitions or code it deploys.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: The loop and its managed components. Configurable through published interfaces; the execution itself is not observable.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: The systems the agent reaches, reached through grants the customer issues.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: Supplied by the platform and configured by the customer — the shared-responsibility shape that defines this archetype.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: End user
nodes.note: Whose identity should reach the tool call, rather than being replaced by the agent's.

nodes.label: External content
nodes.note: Documents, web pages and records the agent reads. The platform's guardrails see it; nothing about it is authenticated.

nodes.label: Application front end
nodes.note: The customer's surface, and where the user's identity is established.

nodes.label: Agent definition or code
nodes.note: Either a declarative agent the provider runs, or the customer's own loop in the provider's runtime. The choice decides which platform guardrails apply automatically and which have to be called explicitly.

nodes.label: Runtime interface
nodes.note: Where agents are invoked and their sessions managed. The published surface; the loop behind it is not inspectable.

nodes.label: Managed tool gateway
nodes.note: A documented service the customer configures directly, not an inferred internal. The provider's brokered path to tools and MCP servers, with scoping and logging supplied. Reached automatically by a declarative agent and only on request by custom code.

nodes.label: Managed memory
nodes.note: A documented, separately addressable and separately billed service, not an inferred internal. Session, user or cross-user scope, selected by configuration. Cross-user scope means one user's content can shape another's turn, and it is a flag rather than a design review.

nodes.label: Managed sandbox
nodes.note: A documented service with its own API and its own isolation guarantee, not an inferred internal. Code interpreter and browser, isolated by the provider. Among the strongest reasons to choose a managed runtime over building the tier.

nodes.label: Customer systems
nodes.note: Records and services the agent reaches, under grants the customer issues to the platform.

nodes.label: Managed agent identity
nodes.note: A first-class, revocable principal per agent. The control most self-built architectures never implement, supplied here as a service — and frequently collapsed back into one shared service principal by teams who do not use it.

nodes.label: Managed policy
nodes.note: Per-invocation authorization expressed in the platform's own policy language. Portable to no other provider.

nodes.label: Managed guardrails
nodes.note: Content and injection filtering, applied automatically to declarative agents and explicitly by custom code. The difference is where most deployments quietly lose coverage.

nodes.label: Managed observability
nodes.note: Traces of steps, tool calls and decisions. The only window into a loop that cannot be read, which makes exporting it a requirement rather than an option.

nodes.label: Managed evaluations
nodes.note: Behaviour testing against the deployed configuration, including adversarial suites.

control.note: The identity established here has to be carried into the runtime, or the agent acts as itself for everyone.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Two identities on one call: the application's, and the user it is acting for. Dropping the second is what turns per-user authorization into a service-wide grant.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: An agent definition is a deployable artifact. Treating it with less rigour than application code is common and unwarranted — it is the thing that decides what the agent may do.
control.title: Artifact integrity

control.note: The platform's guardrail applies automatically to a declarative agent and only on request to custom code — the asymmetry teams most often lose coverage to.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: The scope flag is the whole control. Cross-user scope is a supported configuration and its consequence is that one user's content reaches another's turn.
control.title: Memory scoping

control.note: Provider-operated isolation, which is one of the strongest arguments for this archetype over building the tier.
control.title: Isolation boundary

control.note: Per tool rather than per agent where the platform allows it. This is where the managed identity earns its place, and where collapsing everything onto one principal undoes it.
control.title: Agent identity

control.note: Output handling is still the application's, because only it knows where the text will land.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Distinct and revocable per agent. Available by default here, which is the single biggest governance advantage of the archetype.
control.title: Agent identity

control.note: The customer authors the policy and the provider enforces it inside a loop the customer cannot see — the shared-responsibility shape, with the verification gap that comes with it.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: The most consequential asymmetry on this diagram. Moving to the code escape hatch silently drops guardrails that a declarative agent got for free.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: Export it. A trace that lives only in the provider's console is unavailable to the systems that would correlate it with anything else.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: Gating rather than reporting. An agent definition that has not been evaluated against adversarial input should not reach a production alias.
control.title: Evaluation gate

crossCutting.note: A managed runtime makes agents cheap to create, so the population grows faster than the inventory. The platform's own registry answers this if it is used; nothing else will.

Three identities in play — the application's, the user's and the agent's — and the failure is collapsing them. The platform supplies the machinery to keep them separate and does not require anyone to use it.
The runtime, its memory, its gateway and its sandbox are all the provider's code in the path, released on the provider's schedule, with the customer's agent inside them.

deviations.subject: Three components are drawn inside the vendor zone
deviations.reason: Every other vendor zone in this catalogue contains only the interfaces a provider publishes, because drawing a vendor's internals means inventing them. Here the memory service, the sandbox and the tool gateway are documented, separately addressable and separately billed products, so drawing them is reporting. Each carries an explicit claim to that effect, and the build refuses the claim anywhere it would not be true.

deviations.subject: The runtime is a vendorOpaque zone although the customer operates the system
deviations.reason: This is a cloud archetype and most of it is the customer's. The runtime zone is marked opaque because the loop's execution is genuinely not inspectable — the customer configures it and cannot read it — and marking it as owned would imply a level of control that does not exist.

deviations.subject: Managed guardrails, policy and identity are drawn in the control plane, not the runtime
deviations.reason: The provider operates them, so they could sit in the runtime zone. They are drawn in the control plane because the customer configures them and because their being separately addressable services is the whole shape of this product category — which is also the finding that CoSAI's component taxonomy has nowhere to put any of them.

deviations.subject: The declarative-versus-code choice is drawn as one node
deviations.reason: They are two quite different deployments. They share every other component on the diagram, and the difference is captured where it actually bites — on the guardrail edge, which applies automatically to one and only on request to the other.

archetypes.title: Managed model API consumption
summary: Consuming a cloud provider's hosted models as a dependency of applications the organisation operates. The most common AI architecture there is, and the one most often treated as a library call rather than as a boundary crossing.
description:
This is drawn as its own archetype because it is the shared substrate beneath most of the cloud application archetypes, and because the decisions made here are made once and inherited by all of them. Where a team places the gateway, how the credential is issued, whether guardrails are on the request path and whether the log is complete are properties of this layer, not of each application above it.
The essential move is that the provider is a boundary and the crossing needs one place. A model call made directly from each service with an SDK and a key in a config map produces no complete log, no consistent policy and no single place to rotate. Consolidating on a gateway is what turns a scattered dependency into a governed one, and it is much cheaper before there are twenty callers than after.
The provider-side controls are real and worth using: managed guardrails, abuse monitoring, content filtering and regional routing all exist and all cost less than building equivalents. They are also configuration the consumer authors and the provider enforces — the classic shared responsibility shape — and their defaults are usually permissive.
The three things that catch organisations out are data handling terms, model version churn and cost. What the provider retains and whether it trains on inputs is a contract question with a per-service answer. Model versions are deprecated on the provider's schedule, so pinning and a tested upgrade path are availability controls. And a token-metered dependency with no quota is an open financial commitment reachable from anything that can loop.
distinguishedBy:
Against self-hosted inference: the same capability with the serving tier, the supply chain and the capacity problem on the provider's side. Almost every control in that archetype is replaced here by a contract term and a configuration setting.
Against the AI gateway archetype: that one is about operating the gateway as a platform for many teams and providers. This is about the consuming relationship itself, and the two are usually built in that order.

exemplars.name: Cloud provider model services
exemplars.note: Hyperscaler-hosted model endpoints with managed guardrails, regional routing and account-level data-handling terms, reached with the account's own identity system.

exemplars.name: Direct provider APIs
exemplars.note: A model vendor's own API, reached with a provider-issued key. Fewer platform controls, and the credential is not part of the organisation's existing identity fabric.

zones.note: Content that reaches the prompt from elsewhere, and the users of the applications above.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Every service that wants to call a model. The population this layer exists to serve.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: The one place model traffic crosses out. Its value is entirely in there being exactly one.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: Inference, provider-side guardrails and abuse monitoring. Configurable, not inspectable.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Credentials, quotas, version policy, logging and the contract.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Content reaching the prompt
nodes.note: Whatever the applications above put in context — documents, tickets, tool output. This layer cannot tell trusted from untrusted, which is why guardrails here are a backstop rather than the primary defence.

nodes.label: Application services
nodes.note: Many callers, written by different teams at different times. Whether they can reach the provider directly decides whether this architecture holds.

nodes.label: Prompt assembly
nodes.note: Where the system instruction, the context and the user turn are combined. Owned by each application, and the reason a central guardrail cannot see intent.

nodes.label: Model gateway
nodes.note: One egress point for model traffic: routing, quotas, redaction and a complete log. The difference between a governed dependency and twenty ungoverned ones.

nodes.label: Network egress policy
nodes.note: Default-deny to model endpoints except through the gateway. Without it the gateway is a convention, and conventions do not survive a deadline.

nodes.label: Model endpoint
nodes.note: The published interface, with a version identifier that has a deprecation date attached to it. Everything behind it is the provider's.

nodes.label: Provider guardrails
nodes.note: Managed content and safety filtering, configured by the consumer and enforced by the provider. Cheaper than building an equivalent, and permissive by default.

nodes.label: Credential broker
nodes.note: Short-lived, per-workload credentials rather than a provider key in configuration. Also what makes per-caller attribution possible at the gateway.

nodes.label: Quota and cost policy
nodes.note: Per-caller token and spend limits. A metered dependency with no ceiling is an open financial commitment reachable by anything that can loop.

nodes.label: Model version registry
nodes.note: Which versions are approved, which are pinned, and when each is deprecated by the provider. Version churn is an availability risk on somebody else's schedule.

nodes.label: Version evaluation
nodes.note: Re-testing behaviour when the provider ships a new version. A model upgrade is a dependency upgrade with no changelog anyone can diff.

nodes.label: Usage and prompt log
nodes.note: What was sent, by whom, to which model and at what cost. Complete only because everything goes through one place.

nodes.label: Data handling terms
nodes.note: Retention, training use, region and subprocessors. Per service and per tier, and the answer changes when the provider ships a new product.

control.note: Applied by the consuming application, which is the only party that knows which part of the context it assembled and which arrived from elsewhere.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: The application proves what it is; the provider credential never reaches it. This is what makes per-caller quota and attribution possible at all.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Issued by the broker at call time and expiring. Contrast with a key in configuration, which is the same authority with no expiry and no attribution.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Not observable. The guardrail's decision and the inference both happen inside the boundary.
control.title: Provider-internal

control.note: Transport is authenticated and the content is not. Output handling belongs to the consuming application, because only it knows where the text is about to be rendered or executed.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: One rotation point instead of one per service, which is the practical argument for the gateway.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Enforced at the crossing rather than trusted to each caller. A retry loop in one service should not be able to exhaust the account.
control.title: Quota and rate limit

control.note: Pinning at the gateway means one place to test and roll an upgrade, instead of a coordinated change across every caller.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: A provider version becomes approved by passing tests, not by being available.
control.title: Evaluation gate

control.note: Complete because there is one crossing. A per-service SDK call produces a log that is complete only for the services that remembered to write one.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: The only control over what the provider does with what it receives. Re-read it when the provider ships a new service, because the terms are rarely uniform across their catalogue.
control.title: Contractual assurance

crossCutting.note: Any service that can reach the internet can reach a model provider. Everything on this diagram depends on egress policy making the gateway the only available path.
A metered dependency behind an agent loop. Not attributable to one node — it is what happens when retry logic meets per-token billing without a ceiling.
Model versions change under the consumer on the provider's schedule. Pinning, evaluation and staged rollout together are the answer; any one alone is not.

deviations.subject: The provider zone shows a guardrail as well as an endpoint
deviations.reason: Provider guardrails are usually a separate configurable service rather than part of the inference endpoint, and their configuration is the consumer's. Drawing them as one node would hide a control the consumer actually operates; drawing internals beyond these two would be inventing them.

deviations.subject: Consuming applications are drawn as one node
deviations.reason: There are many, written by different teams. The archetype is the relationship rather than any one caller, and the population problem is stated in the note and in the shadow-AI risk rather than by drawing twenty boxes.

deviations.subject: Data handling terms are drawn as an evaluation-harness node
deviations.reason: A contract is not a harness. The vocabulary has no node type for a legal instrument, and this is the closest match for something that establishes assurance without executing anything. It is drawn because leaving it out would put no control at all on what the provider retains.

archetypes.title: Embedded retrieval assistant
summary: A conversational surface inside an application you operate, answering from your own corpus by retrieving context at query time and grounding a model response in it. The most common production AI architecture, and the one where the index is the trust boundary.
description:
Two pipelines meet at the index and they have different threat models. The ingest pipeline runs offline, reads systems of record, chunks and embeds them, and writes an index. The query pipeline runs per request, retrieves from that index, assembles a prompt, calls a model, and renders an answer. Almost every serious failure in this archetype is a mismatch between what the two pipelines assume.
The index is a second copy of your data with its own permissions model. The source has ACLs that a decade of access reviews has shaped; the index has whatever the ingest pipeline chose to carry over, evaluated at whatever time it last ran. Retrieval-time filtering against live entitlements is the control that keeps the two in step, and building it after the index exists is considerably harder than building it before. An index that is filtered post-retrieval — fetch first, drop what the user may not see — has already put the content in the process that is assembling a prompt.
Retrieved content is untrusted input. It arrives in the same context window as the system instruction and the user's question, and the model has no reliable way to tell them apart. Where the corpus contains anything a third party can write — support tickets, uploaded documents, product reviews, mail — retrieval is an injection path that reaches every user who later asks a related question. Where the assistant can also call tools, that path reaches actions.
The third property worth drawing is that the model is a boundary crossing. Whether inference is a managed API or something you host, the prompt leaves your application tier with whatever context retrieval put into it, and what comes back drives rendering and possibly tool calls. The two handlers on either side of that crossing are where output encoding and grounding checks live, and they are the components most often skipped because the demo worked without them.
distinguishedBy:
Against the tenant-wide vendor assistant: the same user-facing capability with every control point on the opposite side of the boundary. Here you own the index, the retrieval-time ACL check, the guardrails and the logs, and the work is designing them. There you own the grant model and the edges, and the work is assurance. Almost no capability transfers.
Against an autonomous action agent: this archetype answers, that one acts. The distinction is not the model or the retrieval but whether a wrong answer is a wrong answer or a wrong write. Adding a single tool that mutates a record moves an assistant into that archetype and its control set, which is why the boundary between them is worth naming rather than blurring.
Against a text-to-SQL analytics agent: both ground answers in your data, but that one generates a query against live records and the semantic layer is the control, where here the index is.

exemplars.name: In-product help and knowledge assistants
exemplars.note: A panel inside an application answering from that product's documentation and the tenant's own records. The most common shipped form of this archetype.

exemplars.name: Internal knowledge assistants
exemplars.note: Built on a managed model API plus a vector store, over a wiki, a ticket system and a document repository. Usually the first AI system an organisation operates itself, and usually built before anyone has asked the retrieval-time-ACL question.

zones.note: Users, and the third parties whose content ends up in the corpus.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Where requests arrive, are authenticated, and are rate limited.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: The query pipeline. Everything here runs per request with the calling user's context, and everything here is the Application Developer's to instrument.
zones.label: Compute tier · query path

zones.note: The offline half. Runs on a schedule with a service identity, and its permission decisions are frozen into the index until it runs again.
zones.label: Compute tier · ingest

zones.note: The index, the corpus behind it, and the conversation state.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: A managed inference API. Where inference is self-hosted instead, this zone passes to the AI Model Serving persona and the self-hosted inference archetype describes what replaces it.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: The full set, because the operating personas run the system themselves. This is what the equivalent SaaS archetype does not have and cannot obtain.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: End user
nodes.note: An authenticated user of the application, with entitlements the answer must respect.

nodes.label: Third-party content authors
nodes.note: Anyone who can write into an indexed source — a customer filing a ticket, a colleague uploading a file, an external system syncing records. Their text is model input later.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.note: Authenticates the caller, enforces quotas, and is where per-user cost limits belong.

nodes.label: Input handling
nodes.note: Validation and classification of the user's turn before it reaches retrieval. Catches the direct injection attempt and none of the indirect one, which is the more common of the two.

nodes.label: Query orchestration
nodes.note: Assembles the prompt: system instruction, retrieved context, conversation history, user turn. The component that decides what the model is allowed to see.

nodes.label: Retriever
nodes.note: Selects context for this turn. The right place for the entitlement check, because it is the last point at which content can be excluded rather than merely dropped after fetching.

nodes.label: Output handling and encoding
nodes.note: Checks the answer against what was actually retrieved, then encodes it for wherever it lands — markup, a query, a shell, another prompt. Both halves belong to one stage, and both are skipped together when a demo works without them.

nodes.label: Source connectors
nodes.note: Read the systems of record on a schedule, under a service identity whose reach is usually broader than any single user's.

nodes.label: Chunk and embed
nodes.note: Splits, embeds, and writes. Whatever permission metadata is not carried across here cannot be enforced at query time, however good the retriever is.

nodes.label: Systems of record
nodes.note: The authoritative content and the authoritative permissions.

nodes.label: Vector index
nodes.note: A second copy of the corpus with its own permission model and its own freshness. The trust boundary of this archetype, and the asset most worth threat modelling on its own.

nodes.label: Conversation state
nodes.note: Session-scoped and per-user. Cross-user persistence would change this archetype's risk profile substantially, which is why the scope is worth stating rather than assuming.

nodes.label: Inference API
nodes.note: The published interface. What runs behind it is the provider's and is not drawn.

nodes.label: Identity provider
nodes.note: Establishes the user and the entitlements the retriever will filter against.

nodes.label: Secrets broker
nodes.note: Short-lived credentials for the model API and the connectors, issued per workload rather than stored per deployment.

nodes.label: AI gateway and guardrails
nodes.note: One enforcement point in front of every model call: routing, quotas, content policy, and the log of what was actually sent. Drawn inline in the application tier rather than in the control plane, because it is in the request path — a gateway that traffic can go around is not a gateway.

nodes.label: Audit and observability
nodes.note: Prompts, retrieved document ids, model responses and decisions. Retrieved ids are the part most often omitted and the part an investigation needs first.

nodes.label: Evaluation and red teaming
nodes.note: Continuous adversarial testing against the live index, because the corpus changes daily and a pre-launch test result expires with it.

nodes.label: AI posture management
nodes.note: Inventory of models, indexes and endpoints in use, and their configuration drift.

control.note: The existing write path into the system of record. Nothing here knows the content will later be read by a model on behalf of a different user.
control.title: Existing content permissions

control.note: Carries the identity the retriever must filter against; the assistant is only as scoped as this.
control.title: User identity

control.note: The user's identity has to survive this hop or the retriever cannot filter. Dropping to a service identity here is the single most common cause of over-broad retrieval.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Two distinct things: what the service may read, and what this user may see. Only the second is per request, and only the second stops one user's question returning another's document.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: Scope is the control. A cache keyed loosely enough to collide across users leaks by construction.
control.title: Memory scoping

control.note: Issued per workload and expiring. Contrast with the endpoint archetypes, where the same key sits in a file for months.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: The transport is authenticated and the content is not. Everything downstream must treat this as untrusted input, which is what the next two nodes exist for.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Encoding is chosen by where it lands, so this edge's safety is a property of the renderer, not the session.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Broader than any user's access, by design and by necessity. Its scope sets the index's contents and therefore the maximum reach of a retrieval-time filtering mistake.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: No second check between reading a document and embedding it. Whatever permission metadata arrives here is all the index will ever know about that content.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Write access to the index is write access to what every future answer is grounded in. It deserves the scrutiny of a production deploy credential, and rarely gets it.
control.title: Artifact integrity

control.note: The gateway validates signatures against published keys rather than calling the provider. Token lifetime therefore sets how long a revoked entitlement stays usable.
control.title: User identity

control.note: The pipeline proves what it is to the broker and receives a short-lived credential. The long-lived connector grant still exists; it just no longer sits on disk.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: The gateway holds the provider credential so no application service has to. That is the point of putting it in the path: one place to rotate, one place that sees every call.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: The application can write and cannot amend. Without that asymmetry the audit trail shares a compromise with the thing it is meant to record.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: Evaluations that bypass the gateway test a system nobody runs. Sending them through the same enforcement point is what makes the result mean anything.
control.title: Evaluation gate

control.note: Posture tooling enumerates configuration, not content. A posture scanner that can read the index has become part of the data path it was meant to observe.
control.title: Independent discovery

crossCutting.note: Enters at authoring time, through a pipeline that runs days earlier, and surfaces in another user's answer. No node owns it: the ingest pipeline, the index, the retriever and the orchestrator each handle it correctly in isolation and the path still exists.
Produced by the gap between the crawler's standing grant and the retriever's per-request filter. Both are individually defensible; the risk is the distance between them.
Embedding models, vector stores, retrieval libraries and SDKs are all third-party code in the request path, and the index format is a deserialization surface.

deviations.subject: The ingest pipeline is drawn as its own zone rather than part of the application tier
deviations.reason: They usually share infrastructure, so this is not a network boundary. It is drawn separately because the two run at different times, under different identities, with different reach — and the archetype's central failure is the gap between them. A diagram that merges them hides the thing worth seeing.

deviations.subject: Chunk-and-embed uses the tuning-pipeline node type
deviations.reason: The vocabulary has no dedicated ingest-transform type, and the tuning pipeline is the closest honest match: a scheduled build system that produces an artifact the runtime trusts. Both carry the same supply-chain properties.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway is drawn in the application tier, not the control plane
deviations.reason: It is usually bought and operated as a governance product, and its policy is authored there. But it sits in the request path — every model call passes through it — and drawing it beside the flow rather than in it would imply traffic could go around. Its policy source is drawn as a control edge instead.

deviations.subject: The provider zone assumes a managed model API
deviations.reason: Self-hosted inference is equally common and changes the ownership of that zone entirely. It is drawn as a vendor zone because that is the more common case and the more instructive boundary; the self-hosted variant is a separate archetype rather than a footnote here.

archetypes.title: Remote MCP server you publish
summary: A tool server operated as a service for other people's agents. An OAuth resource server whose clients are language models, which is a threat model no API was designed for.
description:
The inversion is what makes this its own architecture. Every other cloud archetype here calls tools; this one is the tool. The caller is an autonomous agent acting for a user, the arguments were produced by a model, and the tool descriptions this server publishes become instructions inside that model's context.
That last point is the responsibility no ordinary API has. A tool description is not documentation — it is text the calling model acts on. A poorly worded description causes misuse; a deliberately worded one is an attack on the caller. Publishing a server means accepting that its descriptions and its error messages are part of somebody else's prompt, and treating changes to them with the seriousness of an API contract change.
Authorization is the second inversion. Standard OAuth answers "may this client act for this user", and here that is necessary and not sufficient: the client is an agent that may have been steered by content it read elsewhere. Scopes therefore need to be narrow enough that a hijacked agent's blast radius is bounded, and consequential operations need confirmation semantics the protocol can express, rather than relying on the client to prompt its user.
The operational shape is otherwise a well-understood multi-tenant service, and the ordinary disciplines apply with unusual force: per-tenant isolation, rate limits sized for machine callers rather than humans, idempotency because agents retry, and output sizing because a large result is both a cost problem for the caller and a way to crowd their context window.
distinguishedBy:
Against a third-party MCP server you consume: opposite side of the same boundary. There the scopes are someone else's design and the work is admission and observation; here the scopes, the tenancy and the descriptions are all design decisions.
Against an AI-augmented API backend: that one has AI inside it and a conventional client. This one has no AI inside it at all and a model as the client. The security work is entirely about the caller's nature, not about anything the service does with a model.
Against the local tool plane: same protocol, no boundary there and a real one here. A remote server has an identity, a grant and an audit trail, which is why it is a considerably better position than a stdio child process.

exemplars.name: Product MCP servers
exemplars.note: SaaS vendors publishing remote tool servers for their own products so customer agents can act without a bespoke integration.

exemplars.name: Internal MCP servers
exemplars.note: The same pattern inside one organisation, exposing internal systems to internal agents. Same architecture, and the temptation to skip the authorization work is much stronger.

zones.note: The calling agents and the users behind them. Neither is under this service's control.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Where agent traffic arrives and is authorised, throttled and logged.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: Tool implementations, and the descriptions that become somebody else's prompt.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: What the tools actually read and write, per tenant.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: Identity, scopes, audit, and the review process for description changes.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Calling agent
nodes.note: Someone else's agent, acting for a user, with arguments composed by a model that may have read hostile content. A non-human caller that is neither a person nor a bot to block.

nodes.label: Delegating user
nodes.note: The person the agent acts for, and the source of the authorization. Not present at call time, which is why consequential operations cannot rely on them being asked.

nodes.label: Authorization server
nodes.note: Issues scoped, expiring tokens to named clients. The one place a compromised agent's access can be withdrawn without redeploying anything.

nodes.label: Protocol endpoint
nodes.note: The published MCP endpoint. Session handling here is a security surface — session identifiers that can be guessed or replayed hand one caller another's context.

nodes.label: Rate and cost limits
nodes.note: Sized for machine callers, which retry, loop and parallelise in ways human clients do not. A limit tuned for people is not a limit here.

nodes.label: Tool definitions
nodes.note: Names, descriptions and schemas. These are not documentation — they are text the calling model treats as instruction, which makes changing them a change to somebody else's prompt.

nodes.label: Tool handlers
nodes.note: The implementations. Arguments arrive model-generated, so validation has to assume plausible nonsense rather than the malformed input a conventional client produces.

nodes.label: Confirmation semantics
nodes.note: Marking an operation as requiring the caller to confirm with its user. The server cannot enforce it, but declaring it is the only lever it has on consequential calls.

nodes.label: Result shaping
nodes.note: Bounding size and structure. An oversized result costs the caller money and crowds their context window, which is a denial-of-service against a model rather than a server.

nodes.label: Tenant data
nodes.note: Per-tenant records the tools reach. Isolation here is the claim consuming organisations cannot verify and will ask about in assurance.

nodes.label: Scope catalogue
nodes.note: What each scope permits. Coarse scopes are the difference between a hijacked agent doing one thing and doing everything the user could.

nodes.label: Description review
nodes.note: Reviewing tool text as a security artifact, because it executes in a caller's context. Rarely done, and the reason a benign-looking copy edit can change how thousands of agents behave.

nodes.label: Call audit
nodes.note: Which client, for which user, called what with which arguments and what came back.

control.note: The user authorises a named client for named scopes. The last point at which a human decides anything in this architecture — every subsequent call happens without them.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Audience restriction matters more than usual: a token that other resource servers accept turns one compromised agent into a multi-service problem.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Establishes the client and the user. It cannot establish whether the agent was steered by content it read elsewhere, which is why scopes and confirmation semantics carry the weight.
control.title: Agent identity

control.note: Client, user and tenant travel with the request rather than being re-derived. A handler that re-resolves the tenant from an argument is trusting a model to name it.
control.title: Brokered credential

edges.label: tool schema into the caller's context

control.note: Tool text is a versioned, reviewed artifact rather than editable copy, because it executes as instruction inside another organisation's model. Changing it is shipping an interface change.
control.title: Verified provenance

control.note: Two checks: the scope permits the operation, and the tenant on the token matches the tenant on the record. Skipping the second is how cross-tenant access happens in practice.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: Same two checks, applied on the read path where the volume is much higher.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: The result enters the caller's context window as content. Size and structure are the server's responsibility to the caller, not a nicety.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Where a hijacked agent's blast radius is actually decided — long before any call arrives.
control.title: Scoped tool permission

control.note: Because the text runs in someone else's model, editing it is closer to shipping an API change than to updating documentation.
control.title: Verified provenance

control.note: Client, user, arguments and result. Also the only way to answer a customer asking what their agent did here.
control.title: Append-only audit

crossCutting.note: This server is on the causing side rather than the suffering side. Its descriptions, its errors and its results all land in a caller's context, so its output hygiene is somebody else's input security.
The token proves a user consented; it cannot prove the agent still represents their intent. Scope design is the whole of the answer, and it happens before any request arrives.
Every read and every write needs the tenant on the token checked against the tenant on the record. It is not one node's job — it is a discipline across all of them.

deviations.subject: The tool-schema edge runs backwards, from this service into the caller
deviations.reason: Every other edge on these diagrams carries a request or a response. This one carries text that becomes instruction in another organisation's model, and it is drawn as a crossing with an auth mechanism of none because that is the honest description: no authentication applies to what a description means.

deviations.subject: No model appears anywhere in this architecture
deviations.reason: There is no AI in this service. It is in the catalogue because its client is a model, and every distinctive control here follows from that and from nothing else.

deviations.subject: Confirmation semantics are drawn in the service tier though the server cannot enforce them
deviations.reason: The server declares that an operation needs the caller to confirm; whether the caller honours it is outside this boundary. It is drawn because declaring it is a real design decision and the only lever available, and its note says plainly that enforcement is not the server's.

archetypes.title: Sandboxed agentic execution service
summary: A service that runs agents in disposable isolated environments — cloud coding agents, autonomous operations agents, agentic browsing. Untrusted code and untrusted instructions execute together, and the isolation is the product.
description:
Everything here follows from one design commitment: the agent is assumed to be compromisable, and the architecture is arranged so that it does not matter very much when it is. The sandbox is not a hardening measure applied to an otherwise-trusted workload; it is the trust boundary the whole service is organised around.
Three properties make the isolation real. The environment is disposable, so persistence is impossible without escaping — a compromise lasts for one task rather than indefinitely. Egress is default-deny with an allowlist, so an agent that has been steered into exfiltrating cannot reach a collection endpoint. And credentials are injected outside the sandbox rather than handed into it, so a compromised agent can use a capability without ever holding the secret that authorises it.
That last property is the one most often skipped and the one that matters most. An agent given a repository token inside its container has a token an injected instruction can exfiltrate. An agent whose git operations are proxied through a component holding the token can push commits and cannot steal the credential. The difference is entirely architectural.
Multi-tenancy at the isolation layer is the remaining hard part. Containers sharing a kernel are a different security claim from microVMs with their own, and running many customers' agents on shared hosts makes the isolation technology a load-bearing security decision rather than an operational one.
The output is where the boundary is crossed on purpose. Whatever the agent produces — a pull request, a configuration change, a report — leaves the sandbox and enters systems that trust it. Review of that artifact is the last control, and it is a human one.
distinguishedBy:
Against the endpoint coding agent: the same loop, hosted. The endpoint version runs on a machine that also holds SSH keys, cloud credentials and a browser profile, and nothing separates them. Here the environment contains nothing but the task, and is destroyed afterwards.
Against the durable multi-agent workflow: that one is about surviving failure across a long process. This one is about containing a compromise inside a short one. A workflow may use this as a step; they are not the same concern.

exemplars.name: Cloud coding agents
exemplars.note: Vendor services that clone a repository into an isolated environment, run an agent against the task, and open a pull request for review.

exemplars.name: Autonomous operations and SRE agents
exemplars.note: Agents given a contained environment and read access to production telemetry, proposing or applying remediations through a reviewed path.

exemplars.name: Agentic browsing services
exemplars.note: Hosted browser automation driven by an agent, where the browser runs in the sandbox rather than in the user's own session.

zones.note: The requester, the repositories and pages the agent reads, and the internet it cannot reach.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Schedules tasks, provisions environments and holds the credentials. Deliberately outside the sandbox, which is the point.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: One task, one environment, destroyed afterwards. Assumed compromised; arranged so that a compromise expires with the task.
zones.label: Isolated execution

zones.note: Repositories, infrastructure and records that will trust the artifact the agent produced.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: The published inference interface.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Identity, egress policy, review and audit.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Task requester
nodes.note: Describes the outcome, and reviews the artifact at the end. Absent in between.

nodes.label: Repository and web content
nodes.note: Code, issues, dependency metadata and pages the agent reads. Assumed hostile, which is why the environment is arranged the way it is rather than filtered.

nodes.label: Arbitrary internet
nodes.note: Where a compromised agent would send what it found. Drawn because the default-deny egress policy exists precisely to make this edge fail.

nodes.label: Task scheduler
nodes.note: Accepts work, provisions an environment per task, and tears it down at the end.

nodes.label: Credential broker
nodes.note: Holds the tokens the task needs and never passes them inward. The agent gets a capability; the secret stays outside the blast radius.

nodes.label: Action proxy
nodes.note: Performs the privileged operations on the agent's behalf — the push, the API call, the deployment. Where credential isolation actually happens rather than being asserted.

nodes.label: Agent loop
nodes.note: Plans and executes inside the environment, with no standing authority of its own.

nodes.label: Workspace, shell and browser
nodes.note: Filesystem, toolchain and a browser with no pre-existing sessions. Contains the task and nothing else — no other repository, no other customer, no long-lived state, and none of the user's own authenticated sessions.

nodes.label: Egress allowlist
nodes.note: Default-deny with a per-task allowlist. The control that makes a successful injection unprofitable rather than merely detected.

nodes.label: Reviewed artifact
nodes.note: The pull request, change or report the work produces. The one thing that crosses out deliberately, and the last place a human is in the loop.

nodes.label: Repositories and infrastructure
nodes.note: Systems that will trust the artifact once someone merges or applies it.

nodes.label: Inference API
nodes.note: Reached through the egress allowlist like everything else the sandbox talks to.

nodes.label: Isolation and egress policy
nodes.note: Which isolation technology, which allowlist, which resource ceiling. Whether tenants share a kernel is a security decision that often gets made as an operational one.

nodes.label: Artifact review
nodes.note: A human reading the diff before it lands. The last control, and the one that erodes fastest as volume grows.

nodes.label: Session audit
nodes.note: Prompts, commands, network attempts and proxied actions. Denied egress attempts are the most useful signal on this diagram and the one most often not collected.

nodes.label: Task termination
nodes.note: Destroying the environment. Cheap here in a way it is nowhere else in this catalogue, because the environment was disposable by design.

control.note: The requester's entitlements bound what the broker will later be willing to do for the task.
control.title: User identity

control.note: A fresh identity per task, expiring with it. Persistence across tasks would undo the main property this architecture is built for.
control.title: Isolation boundary

control.note: Assumed hostile on arrival. The architecture does not try to make this content safe; it makes the environment that reads it disposable.
control.title: Isolation boundary

control.note: On the allowlist, and the credential comes from outside. Even the model call does not put a secret inside the environment.
control.title: Egress allowlist

control.note: Drawn because it fails. Making exfiltration unprofitable is a stronger position than making injection unlikely, and it is the one this architecture can actually achieve.
control.title: Egress allowlist

control.note: The defining crossing. The agent asks for an effect; the proxy holds the credential and performs it. A compromised agent gets the capability and never the secret.
control.title: Credential isolation

control.note: The proxy can never exceed what the requester could have done, which keeps delegation from becoming escalation.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: The work leaves as a reviewable artifact rather than as a direct change, which is what keeps the human gate at the end meaningful.
control.title: Credential isolation

control.note: The last control. Erodes as volume grows, which is the practical argument for keeping everything upstream of it strong.
control.title: Human approval

control.note: Deliberately the same path a human's change takes, so the existing review, CI and deployment controls apply unchanged.
control.title: Human approval

control.note: Enforced by the platform rather than configured inside the thing being contained. A sandbox that can reach its own configuration is not one.
control.title: Isolation boundary

control.note: Per task rather than per service, so a task's reach matches its actual dependencies.
control.title: Egress allowlist

control.note: Denied attempts are the highest-value signal in this archetype — they are what a successful injection looks like when the architecture worked.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: Cheap and complete, because the environment was disposable from the start.
control.title: Emergency stop

crossCutting.note: Not mitigated here, contained. The architecture assumes the agent will be steered and is arranged so the consequences expire with the task and cannot reach the network.
Whether tenants share a kernel, a host or a network path is decided by the isolation technology rather than by any component on the diagram, and it is the claim customers will ask about.
Reduced to what the proxy will perform and what a reviewer will merge. The agent's own authority is deliberately nil, which is what makes the remaining surface small enough to reason about.

deviations.subject: The credential broker and action proxy are drawn in the orchestration tier, not the sandbox
deviations.reason: Their placement is the architecture. Drawing them anywhere else would describe a different and much weaker system, and the whole credential-isolation property is a statement about which side of the boundary they sit on.

deviations.subject: A denied egress edge is drawn
deviations.reason: Diagrams normally show what happens, not what is prevented. This one is drawn because the default-deny policy is the archetype's most important control and it has no other visible effect — a control whose success looks like nothing happening needs to be shown failing.

deviations.subject: The sandbox zone is attributed to the Platform Provider persona
deviations.reason: The agent logic belongs to the Agentic Platform persona and the code belongs to the developer, but the isolation guarantee — the actual security property — is the platform's. Attributing the zone to whoever wrote the code inside it would misplace the responsibility.

archetypes.title: Self-hosted open-weights inference
summary: Open-weights models served on infrastructure the organisation operates — GPU nodes, a serving runtime, a router in front. Chosen for data residency, cost or control, and it moves the entire model-provider role inside the boundary.
description:
The trade is explicit and worth stating before the diagram: a data-disclosure risk goes away and a supply-chain, availability and safety risk arrives. There is no provider applying content policy, no provider absorbing a traffic spike, and no provider patching the serving stack. The AI Model Serving persona becomes an internal one.
The supply chain is the distinctive risk. Weights are large artifacts from public hubs, and several distribution formats execute code on load. The control is scanning and format policy in the promotion pipeline, before an artifact reaches a node — not after, and not as a report. A registry with provenance and a promotion gate is what separates this from the endpoint variant of the same software.
Multi-tenancy on accelerators is the risk that has no equivalent anywhere else in this catalogue. Batching mixes tenants' requests in one forward pass, the KV cache holds their context, and prefix caching across tenants is a performance feature that is also a disclosure path. Whether cache entries can be shared across tenants is a serving-configuration question with data-protection consequences, and it is rarely reviewed as one.
Availability becomes a security property here in a way it is not with a managed API. GPU capacity is finite and expensive, admission control is the only thing standing between one caller and everyone else's latency, and there is no provider to absorb the spike. Quotas are a control, not a billing feature.
distinguishedBy:
Against the endpoint local runtime: identical software, entirely different operational position. There it was installed by one person and has no inventory entry; here it has a pipeline, a network policy, an identity and someone on call. Same risks, opposite maturity.
Against consuming a managed model API: this archetype replaces one boundary crossing with a whole subsystem. The guardrails, abuse monitoring, capacity management and patching that the provider was doing are now components on the diagram.

exemplars.name: Serving runtimes on Kubernetes
exemplars.note: Open-source inference servers with continuous batching and paged attention, scheduled onto GPU node pools with an inference-aware gateway in front.

exemplars.name: On-premises inference for data residency
exemplars.note: The same stack in a datacentre because the data cannot leave. The most common non-cost reason organisations take on this archetype.

zones.note: The public model hubs the weights come from.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: The internal applications and agents calling this service. Multiple tenants of one cluster, which is where the accelerator-sharing questions come from.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: GPU nodes, the runtime and the router. The role a model provider plays in every other cloud archetype, brought inside.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: The registry and the weights, and the promotion decisions between them.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: Scanning, evaluation, quotas, and the guardrails no provider is supplying.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Public model hub
nodes.note: Where open weights are published. Publisher identity is verifiable to a degree; what an artifact does on load is a property of its format, not its publisher.

nodes.label: Consuming applications
nodes.note: Internal callers sharing one cluster. Their isolation from each other is a property of the serving configuration, not of the network between them.

nodes.label: Inference gateway
nodes.note: Model routing, admission control and per-tenant quotas. On finite GPU capacity, admission control is what stops one caller becoming everyone else's outage.

nodes.label: Serving runtime
nodes.note: Continuous batching, paged attention, KV cache. The batching that makes it efficient is also what puts several tenants' context in one process.

nodes.label: KV and prefix cache
nodes.note: Holds recent context to avoid recomputing it. Sharing prefixes across tenants is a performance feature and a disclosure path, and the choice between them is a configuration flag that rarely reaches a review.

nodes.label: Loaded models on GPU
nodes.note: The weights in memory across a node pool. Also a high-value exfiltration target: the artifact is expensive and portable.

nodes.label: Model registry
nodes.note: Versioned artifacts with provenance and a promotion gate. The single control that separates this archetype from the endpoint one running the same software.

nodes.label: Weight storage
nodes.note: Multi-gigabyte artifacts at rest. Encryption and access control here protect an asset that is both expensive to reproduce and trivial to copy.

nodes.label: Artifact scanning
nodes.note: Format and content inspection in the promotion pipeline, before an artifact can reach a node. A scan that runs after deployment has documented an incident.

nodes.label: Guardrail service
nodes.note: Content and intent classification. Drawn in the control plane because with no provider applying policy, this is a service the organisation now runs itself or does without.

nodes.label: Evaluation and red teaming
nodes.note: Safety and adversarial testing per model version, because the provider's evaluation no longer applies to an artifact fetched from a hub and served directly.

nodes.label: Posture and inventory
nodes.note: Which model versions are serving where, at what configuration, with what drift.

nodes.label: Workload identity
nodes.note: Short-lived credentials for callers and for the pipeline that promotes artifacts.

control.note: Establishes who published it. Says nothing about what it does on load, which is why the scanner sits between this edge and any node that will open the file.
control.title: Verified provenance

control.note: The tenant on the token is what the quota and the cache-isolation decisions key off. A request that arrives without one gets whatever the default tenant can do.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Inline rather than advisory. With no provider applying content policy, a guardrail the traffic can go around is not one.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: Verifying the digest at load is what makes registry promotion meaningful. Without it the gate can be bypassed by writing to storage directly.
control.title: Artifact integrity

control.note: The response is unfiltered unless the guardrail is on the return path too. Output-side policy is the half most often omitted when self-hosting.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: A gate rather than a report. This is the single most load-bearing control in the archetype and its value is entirely in being blocking.
control.title: Artifact integrity

control.note: Per version, because a new checkpoint from the same publisher is a new model with new behaviour and no provider is testing it on anyone's behalf.
control.title: Evaluation gate

control.note: Watches serving configuration, including whether cross-tenant cache sharing is on. A posture tool that can read the cache has joined the data path it was meant to observe.
control.title: Independent discovery

control.note: Tenant identity comes from the platform rather than from a shared key in a config map.
control.title: Workload identity

crossCutting.note: Batching, the KV cache and the node pool all mix tenants. Isolation is a property of several configuration choices at once rather than a component anyone deploys.
Spans the hub, the registry, storage and the loader. Format policy in the pipeline is the only place it can be addressed for all four at once.
GPU capacity is finite and there is no provider to absorb a spike. Admission control stops being a billing feature and becomes an availability control.

deviations.subject: The guardrail service sits in the control plane rather than inline
deviations.reason: It is in the request path and the AI-gateway archetype draws its equivalent inline. Here it is drawn as a control-plane service reached by the router, because when self-hosting it is a separate thing the organisation stands up rather than a feature of the serving stack — and showing it as a dependency rather than a built-in is the point.

deviations.subject: The KV cache is drawn as a memory store
deviations.reason: It is an optimisation, not a datastore anyone designed to hold data. It is given a node because cross-tenant prefix sharing puts one tenant's context where another's request can reach it, and a risk with no node has nowhere to attach.

deviations.subject: No end user appears
deviations.reason: This archetype's callers are other systems. The humans are several layers up in whichever application archetype is consuming it, and drawing them here would blur the boundary this diagram exists to show.

archetypes.title: Fine-tuning and model registry pipeline
summary: A build system whose artifact is a model. Curated data goes in, a tuned checkpoint comes out, and everything that is true of a compiler and its supply chain is true here — except that the output cannot be diffed and the defects cannot be found by reading it.
description:
Treating this as a build pipeline is the whole of the correct framing. It has source inputs, a build environment, dependencies, an artifact, a registry and a promotion path, and it deserves the controls a software pipeline gets: reproducibility, provenance, signed artifacts, and a promotion gate nothing bypasses.
Where the analogy breaks is inspection. A compiled binary can be decompiled, diffed and scanned; a tuned checkpoint cannot be read for backdoors in any practical sense. That makes input control and evaluation the substitutes for code review — what went into the training set and how the result behaves are the only two things anyone can actually examine.
Poisoning is therefore the primary risk and it is durable. A poisoned example influences every inference the model ever makes, survives redeployment, and is not removable without retraining. A targeted poisoning that only activates on a trigger phrase is invisible to accuracy metrics and to any evaluation that does not know what to look for.
Training data is also a disclosure surface in a way inference data is not. Memorised examples can be extracted from the model afterwards, so anything with personal or confidential content in the training set has been baked into an artifact that may be shared far more widely than the dataset ever was.
The two access questions to settle early: who may promote a checkpoint to production, and who may read the training corpus. Both tend to default to a broad platform-team role, and both are higher-privilege than they look.
distinguishedBy:
Against the batch pipeline: same build-system trust properties, different artifact. That produces data; this produces a model. The data can be corrected in place, the model cannot.
Against self-hosted inference: that consumes artifacts, this produces them. They meet at the registry, and the promotion gate between them is where both archetypes' supply-chain controls concentrate.

exemplars.name: Managed fine-tuning services
exemplars.note: Provider-hosted tuning against a customer dataset, producing a private checkpoint served from the same platform. Availability of this varies sharply by provider and by year.

exemplars.name: Self-operated tuning on accelerator fleets
exemplars.note: Adapter or full fine-tuning on the organisation's own hardware, with a registry and promotion pipeline built alongside.

exemplars.name: Adapter and preference tuning
exemplars.note: Lightweight tuning producing an adapter rather than a full checkpoint. Smaller artifact, same supply-chain questions, and an additional one about who may load an adapter at serve time.

zones.note: Where training content originated, and the base models the pipeline starts from.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Curation, filtering and labelling. The only place a poisoned example can still be caught.
zones.label: Compute tier · data preparation

zones.note: A build environment with accelerators. Its dependencies, its network reach and its reproducibility are build-system concerns.
zones.label: Compute tier · training

zones.note: The corpus and the artifacts produced from it, both requiring provenance that survives.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: Provenance, evaluation, promotion authority and the record of what produced what.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Training content origins
nodes.note: Scraped corpora, purchased datasets, user-generated content and internal records. Each carries a different provenance claim and most carry none.

nodes.label: Base model
nodes.note: The starting checkpoint. Everything it already contains is inherited, and tuning does not remove it.

nodes.label: Curation and filtering
nodes.note: Deduplication, quality filtering, removal of sensitive content. The last point at which a poisoned or improperly sourced example can be removed rather than baked in.

nodes.label: Labelling and preference data
nodes.note: Human or model-generated labels, frequently from an outsourced workforce. A supply chain with a direct path into model behaviour and almost no scrutiny.

nodes.label: Training job
nodes.note: The build. Reproducibility — same data, same code, same seed, same artifact — is what makes an incident investigable at all.

nodes.label: Frameworks and dependencies
nodes.note: Training libraries and their transitive dependencies, executing with access to the corpus and the artifact. An ordinary software supply chain in an unusual position.

nodes.label: Training corpus
nodes.note: The assembled dataset. Read access to it is higher-privilege than it looks, because it is the union of everything the organisation decided a model should learn.

nodes.label: Tuned checkpoint
nodes.note: The output. Cannot be read for defects, may have memorised its inputs, and will be served to everyone once promoted.

nodes.label: Model registry
nodes.note: Versioned artifacts with lineage back to the exact dataset and code that produced them, and a promotion gate to production.

nodes.label: Data and model lineage
nodes.note: Which examples, which code, which base model, which run. The only route to scoping the damage when a dataset turns out to have been poisoned or improperly sourced.

nodes.label: Evaluation and red teaming
nodes.note: Capability, safety and backdoor probing. Substitutes for reading the artifact, and a targeted poisoning passes every benchmark that does not know its trigger.

nodes.label: Promotion authority
nodes.note: Who may move a checkpoint to production. A high-privilege decision that usually defaults to a broad platform-team role.

nodes.label: Artifact signing
nodes.note: Signing the checkpoint and verifying the signature at load. What makes the registry's promotion gate meaningful rather than advisory.

nodes.label: Memorisation and privacy testing
nodes.note: Extraction and membership-inference testing. The only way to find out whether the artifact remembers its training data before someone else does.

control.note: Curation is the only place a poisoned or improperly sourced example can still be removed. After training it is in the weights and cannot be taken out.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: Frequently an outsourced workforce with a direct influence on model behaviour and very little scrutiny relative to that influence.
control.title: Verified provenance

control.note: Corpus writes decide what the model will learn. The write path deserves the review a production deploy gets.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: Everything already in the base model is inherited. Tuning adds behaviour and does not subtract it.
control.title: Artifact integrity

control.note: Scoped to the dataset approved for this run, so a job cannot quietly widen its own inputs.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: Executes with access to the corpus and the artifact. An ordinary dependency chain with an unusually valuable reach.
control.title: Artifact integrity

control.note: Write-once and candidate-only, so a job cannot overwrite an already-promoted artifact. The signing key lives outside this environment for the same reason.
control.title: Artifact integrity

control.note: The substitute for code review on an artifact nobody can read. Blocking, because a report on an unreadable artifact changes nothing on its own.
control.title: Evaluation gate

control.note: Before promotion, because a model that memorised its training data has turned a dataset with restricted access into an artifact with broad access.
control.title: Evaluation gate

control.note: Outside, so a compromised training job cannot sign its own output. The verification happens at load in whichever serving archetype consumes it.
control.title: Verified provenance

control.note: Separation of duties: whoever runs training should not be able to promote unilaterally. The default configuration usually grants both to the same role.
control.title: Human approval

control.note: Recorded during the run rather than reconstructed later. Without it, a poisoning discovered months on cannot be scoped to affected models.
control.title: Verified provenance

crossCutting.note: The archetype's defining risk, and durable in a way no other archetype's is. It enters at curation or labelling, is baked into an unreadable artifact, and cannot be removed without retraining. Input control and evaluation are the only two places it can be addressed.
Spans origins, labelling and curation, and becomes irreversible at the training job. A licensing or privacy defect discovered afterwards is a retraining decision, not a deletion.
Training data can be memorised and later extracted, so restricted-access content becomes part of a widely-served artifact. This is the disclosure path with no runtime control at all.

deviations.subject: The training environment names the legacy Model Creator persona
deviations.reason: CoSAI marks Model Creator as superseded and the current set has no exact replacement for whoever builds a model. Model Provider describes the party that supplies one, which is not the same as the party that trains it. The legacy persona is the accurate label, and using the nearest current one would misattribute the responsibility.

deviations.subject: Labelling is drawn as a connector
deviations.reason: It is usually an outsourced human workforce, and the vocabulary has no node type for people as a supply chain. Connector captures what matters architecturally — a standing integration feeding data in from a third party — and the note says what it actually is.

deviations.subject: No inference or serving appears
deviations.reason: This archetype ends at the registry. What happens next is the self-hosted inference or managed model archetype, and the promotion gate is the seam between them — drawn here because this is the side that produces the artifact.
