archetypes.title: Realtime voice agent
summary: A conversational agent over a live audio channel, handling calls and acting on what it hears. Injection arrives as speech, the caller's identity is asserted by a voice, and there is no moment to pause and check anything.
description:
Realtime changes what is possible rather than what is at stake. Every asynchronous archetype can insert a filter, a check or a human between the input and the effect. Here the budget is a few hundred milliseconds before the pause becomes audible and the conversation breaks, which means guardrails have to be streaming and partial, and human approval means transferring the call rather than blocking on a queue.
Identity is the harder problem. A voice is not an authenticator and has not been one for several years, so anything consequential needs a second factor on another channel — a code to the registered device, a callback, an in-app confirmation. Systems that treat the calling number plus a plausible voice as authentication are the ones this archetype's incidents come from.
Audio is also the worst medium for detection. Speech-to-text loses tone, homophones and overlapping speakers, so the transcript the guardrail inspects is not what was said. Where only the transcript is retained, an investigation cannot recover what actually happened, and where audio is retained, that is biometric data with its own regulatory weight.
The telephony edge brings risks the rest of the catalogue does not have. Caller identification is spoofable, the network is a third party, and a voice agent reachable on a public number is an always-open endpoint with per-minute inference costs behind it.
distinguishedBy:
Against the autonomous action agent: the same act-on-a-request shape with the latency budget removed. Every deliberative control that archetype relies on — filtering, approval queues, reconsideration — is unavailable, so the compensating controls move to identity and to reversibility.
Against a text chat assistant: the medium changes the threat model. Audio cannot be reliably inspected, transcription is lossy, the caller is anonymous by default, and the recording is biometric data.

exemplars.name: Realtime speech APIs with tool calling
exemplars.note: Provider APIs handling speech in and out with low latency and function calling in-session, increasingly with direct telephony integration.

exemplars.name: Contact-centre voice agents
exemplars.note: Agents answering customer calls end to end, with escalation to a human and access to account records. The mainstream commercial deployment of this archetype.

zones.note: The caller, whoever they actually are, arriving over a network nobody here controls.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Carrier and session border. Caller identification arrives here already untrustworthy, and the network itself is a third party.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: The live conversation, its tools, and whatever can be checked inside the latency budget.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: Customer records the agent reaches, and the audio and transcripts the call produces. The second is biometric data.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: Streaming speech-to-speech inference, holding the audio for the duration of the call.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Identity verification, action limits, retention policy and post-call review.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Caller
nodes.note: Claims an identity by speaking. A voice is not an authenticator and a calling number is spoofable, so this claim needs corroboration before anything consequential happens.

nodes.label: Spoken content
nodes.note: Instructions arriving as audio. Reaches the model with no marker separating it from the system prompt, and cannot be filtered as reliably as text.

nodes.label: Session border
nodes.note: Where the call arrives. Carries caller identification that is spoofable and should be treated as a hint rather than a fact.

nodes.label: Stream handling
nodes.note: Audio in, audio out, continuously. Any inspection here has a few hundred milliseconds before the pause is audible and the conversation stops working.

nodes.label: Dialogue agent
nodes.note: Holds the conversation and decides when to call a tool. Its decisions land in real time with no opportunity to reconsider.

nodes.label: Streaming guardrail
nodes.note: Partial-transcript classification, inbound and outbound. Necessarily weaker than a batch filter, because it must decide before the utterance is finished.

nodes.label: In-session tools
nodes.note: Account lookups and transactions invoked mid-conversation. The gap between reads and writes is where the verification requirement belongs.

nodes.label: Human transfer
nodes.note: Escalation to a person. This archetype's only form of human oversight — a queue is not available when the caller is on the line.

nodes.label: Customer records
nodes.note: What the agent reads and changes, scoped to whoever the caller has actually been proven to be.

nodes.label: Audio and transcripts
nodes.note: Biometric data with its own regulatory weight, plus a transcript that is not a faithful record of what was said. Retaining both has consequences; retaining neither leaves incidents unreconstructable.

nodes.label: Realtime inference
nodes.note: Streaming speech in and out. Holds the audio for the duration of the call, which makes the provider's retention terms a biometric-data question.

nodes.label: Out-of-band verification
nodes.note: A code to the registered device, a callback, an in-app confirmation. The substitute for an authenticator, and required before anything consequential.

nodes.label: Action limits
nodes.note: What may happen on a call with only a voice behind it, and what requires verification or a human. The compensating control for everything realtime makes impossible.

nodes.label: Retention policy
nodes.note: How long audio and transcripts are kept, and who may replay them. A genuine tension between investigability and biometric-data minimisation, with no configuration that satisfies both.

nodes.label: Post-call review
nodes.note: Sampled review of transcripts and actions after the fact. The only deliberative control available, and it arrives after the effect.

control.note: Caller identification is a hint, not an authenticator. Identity is established by the out-of-band factor before anything consequential; this edge carries fraud signals and rate limits only.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Streaming classification on partial transcripts. Necessarily weaker than a batch filter — it must decide before the utterance ends — which is why action limits carry the rest.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: Secures the media path and says nothing about who is speaking. The carrier is a third party in the middle of every call.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Carries the caller's audio for the duration of the call. Retention terms on this path are a biometric-data question rather than a general privacy one.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Outbound guardrails have the same latency budget as inbound ones, so what is checked on the way out is less than anyone would like.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Scoped to what the caller has actually been proven to be, not to what they said they are. Reads on an unverified call should be narrower than reads on a verified one.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: Biometric data plus a lossy transcript. Both need access control on replay, not only on storage.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: The compensating control for an unauthenticated medium. Consequential actions wait for it; conversation does not.
control.title: Delegated grant

edges.label: what a voice alone may do

control.note: Per call rather than per session, because verification may complete partway through a conversation and the permitted set changes when it does.
control.title: Per-invocation policy

control.note: The unresolvable tension of the archetype: keeping audio makes incidents investigable and makes the organisation a custodian of biometric data.
control.title: Data entitlement

control.note: Deliberation after the fact, because there was none during. Reviewer access to recordings is itself worth logging.
control.title: Append-only audit

crossCutting.note: A voice is not an authenticator and a calling number is spoofable, so every action taken on an unverified call is taken for someone who has not been identified. No node fixes this; the out-of-band factor works around it.

Arrives as speech, into a channel that cannot be inspected as reliably as text, within a latency budget too short for a thorough check. All three at once, which is why this archetype leans on limiting consequence rather than filtering input.

Three paths: what the agent reads out to an unverified caller, what the audio sends to the provider, and what the retained recording holds. The third is biometric and outlives the call by whatever the retention policy says.

deviations.subject: Recordings are drawn as a memory store
deviations.reason: They are an operational artifact rather than agent memory. The memory type is used because the security properties match — durable, replayable, holding conversation content — and because it puts the biometric-retention question somewhere visible rather than in prose.

deviations.subject: Human transfer is drawn in the session tier rather than the control plane
deviations.reason: Every other archetype draws its human gate as a governance control. Here it is inside the session because it is not a gate: it is a transfer, happening live, and drawing it as an approval checkpoint would imply a pause that the medium does not permit.

deviations.subject: The telephony edge is attributed to the Platform Provider persona
deviations.reason: The carrier is a third party and could reasonably be an opaque vendor zone. It is drawn as an operated network tier because the session border is configured by the operating organisation, and because its security-relevant property — that caller identification is untrustworthy — is a fact to state rather than a boundary to draw.

archetypes.title: Agentic browser and AI extension
summary: An agent driving a browser that is already logged into everything, or an extension reading every page the user opens. The page is simultaneously the untrusted input and the privileged context, which is what makes this archetype structurally different from the rest.
description:
Every other endpoint archetype has some separation between the content it reads and the authority it holds. Here there is none: the agent acts inside a session that is already authenticated to the user's mail, bank, source control and internal applications, and the instruction it is following arrives as text on a page served by whoever owns that page.
Two variants share the shape. A dedicated agentic browser drives the session itself, with navigation and clicking as tools. An extension sits in the page and reads the DOM, sometimes with permission to act on it. The extension variant is the broader exposure in practice — an extension with host permissions on all sites sees every page including the ones the user would never point an agent at, and its update channel is a supply chain nobody enrolled.
Same-origin policy is the boundary the web is built on, and this archetype's job is to cross it. An agent that reads a page from one origin and then acts on another has done exactly what a decade of browser security is designed to prevent, with the user's cookies attached. There is no browser-level control that distinguishes an agent's cross-origin action from the user's, because from the browser's perspective they are the same session.
The controls that work are the ones that constrain what the session can reach rather than what the agent may say. A separate browser profile with a narrow set of logged-in origins is worth more than any prompt filter, because it converts an unbounded blast radius into a bounded one. In-browser inspection is the only place with visibility into what the agent actually saw and did, which is why browser detection and response is the primary capability here rather than a supporting one.
distinguishedBy:
Against a coding agent: that one reads a repository the developer chose and acts on a filesystem. This one reads pages an attacker serves and acts through credentials the user already holds, with no working directory to scope it to.
Against a desktop assistant with computer use: overlapping and often the same product, but the browser variant is worth separating because its authority is a set of authenticated web sessions rather than local files, and because the extension form has an update channel and a permission model the desktop form does not.

exemplars.name: Agentic browsers
exemplars.note: Browsers with a built-in agent that navigates, reads and clicks on the user's behalf inside their existing signed-in session.

exemplars.name: Assistant sidebars in mainstream browsers
exemplars.note: An assistant panel with access to the current page's content, and increasingly to act on it. Ships enabled to a very large installed base.

exemplars.name: AI browser extensions
exemplars.note: Third-party extensions requesting host permissions across all sites. The permission grant is one click, the update channel is automatic, and the reviewer is the store.

zones.note: The web. Every page is authored by someone else, and the agent reads all of them with the same standing.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: The browser process, its profile, and whatever inspects them.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: The origins the profile is already signed in to. Shared ownership because the authority is granted by each of those applications, not by anything on this device.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: Where page content goes to be reasoned about.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: What an organisation can still enforce on a browser it manages.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: User
nodes.note: Sets the goal, and is usually not reading the pages the agent reads.

nodes.label: Web page content
nodes.note: Visible text, hidden text, alt attributes, comments and anything else in the DOM. All of it is model input, and none of it is distinguishable from the user's instruction once in context.

nodes.label: Extension distribution
nodes.note: Where the extension came from and where its updates come from. An automatic update channel into a component with permission to read every page.

nodes.label: Browser runtime
nodes.note: Navigation, DOM reading and clicking, offered to the model as tools. Its authority is the profile's cookie jar.

nodes.label: Agent loop
nodes.note: Reads the page, decides the next navigation or click, and repeats.

nodes.label: Page extraction
nodes.note: Turns a rendered page into context. The only point where hidden and off-screen content can be stripped before it becomes instruction, and the point most implementations skip.

nodes.label: Action confirmation
nodes.note: Blocks before a consequential click — a purchase, a send, a permission change. The set of actions that count is a product decision and is usually narrower than users assume.

nodes.label: Browser profile
nodes.note: Cookies, saved passwords and session tokens for every origin the user has signed into. Narrowing this to a dedicated profile is the highest-value control in the archetype, and it is a configuration choice rather than a product feature.

nodes.label: In-browser inspection
nodes.note: The only vantage point that sees what the agent read and what it clicked. Where the agent is a vendor's, this is also the only telemetry available.

nodes.label: Signed-in applications
nodes.note: Mail, banking, source control, internal tools. The agent acts on these as the user, and the applications cannot tell the difference.

nodes.label: Inference API
nodes.note: Receives page content, which is frequently more than the user realises they shared.

nodes.label: Extension and browser policy
nodes.note: Managed browser policy: which extensions may install, which origins the agent may reach, and whether the assistant is enabled at all.

nodes.label: Secure service edge
nodes.note: Inline inspection of where the browser goes and what leaves with it.

control.note: The user states an outcome; the pages that determine how it is reached are not theirs.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Hidden and off-screen content stripped before the page becomes context. Bounds the injection rather than preventing it, which is why the profile's scope matters more.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: A signature proves who shipped it, not what it does. An extension with host permissions on all sites is one silent update away from reading every page.
control.title: Verified provenance

control.note: Carries whatever the extraction step passed through, which on an authenticated page is the user's own data.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: The response selects a click. Transport integrity says nothing about whose intent it encodes.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: A dedicated profile with a narrow set of signed-in origins. Converts unbounded ambient authority into a bounded set, and is worth more than any prompt-level control here.
control.title: Credential isolation

control.note: Enforced by the browser against the user, which is the one control here that does not depend on the agent behaving.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: Sees the destinations. Sees the content only where inspection is actually terminated.
control.title: Device posture and inspection

crossCutting.note: Not localisable to a node because the untrusted input and the privileged context are the same object. Every control in this archetype is a mitigation of consequence rather than of cause.
The browser holds authority the agent did not earn and the visited page did not deserve. Every authenticated origin in the profile is in scope for every page the agent reads.
Page content leaves for inference, and the pages are authenticated ones. The user consented to an assistant, not to a transcript of their mail.

deviations.subject: Authenticated sessions are drawn as a zone, and marked shared
deviations.reason: They are not infrastructure and they are not on the device — they are standing grants held by other applications, and the browser merely presents them. Giving them a zone is what makes the blast radius visible; marking them shared is what makes it clear the device owner is not the only party who can revoke.

deviations.subject: The dedicated browser and the extension are drawn as one archetype
deviations.reason: Their trust boundaries and their controls are the same: untrusted page in, ambient authority out, inspection only in the browser. The extension's distribution channel is the one genuine difference and it is drawn as its own node rather than a second diagram.

deviations.subject: Page extraction is drawn even though many products have no such step
deviations.reason: Drawing only what is commonly implemented would leave no place to attach the mitigation. It is drawn with a note saying it is frequently skipped, which is a more useful statement than its absence.

archetypes.title: Vendor coding and coworker agent
summary: A vendor-built agent loop in a terminal or editor, driven by a developer who is present, with read and write access to a working tree, a shell, and whatever tool servers the project admits.
description:
The defining property is the human in the loop and the fact that the loop is scoped to a task. The developer starts it, watches it, and is the approval gate for the actions that matter. Most of this archetype's security posture rests on that gate being real rather than nominal.
What makes it more than an editor plugin is the tool plane. The agent reads a project configuration file to decide which tool servers to launch and trust, and that file usually sits in the repository — which means it arrives with the code. Cloning a project and starting the agent can register tool providers the developer never chose, and the disclosed vulnerability pattern in this archetype is overwhelmingly about that file: injecting into it, swapping its contents after approval, or getting it auto-registered without a prompt. Agent configuration is now a protected-path class, and the vendors that added enforcement did so reactively.
The second exposure is that everything the agent reads is untrusted input with the same standing as the developer's instruction: source files, dependency manifests, issue text, test output, and the responses of any tool it calls. A repository is a document the attacker may have contributed to. The agent has no reliable way to separate the code it was asked to change from instructions embedded in that code.
Approval fatigue is the failure mode that makes the rest matter. A gate that fires on every file write trains the developer to accept, and an accepted prompt is not oversight. The architectures that hold up narrow what needs approving — by sandboxing execution, by scoping tool permissions in advance, and by making network egress default-deny — so that the prompts that do fire are rare enough to read.
distinguishedBy:
Against the personal autonomous harness: this agent is invoked, not triggered; reads content the developer chose to clone, not messages from strangers; holds credentials the vendor issued for a session, not long-lived keys in a dotfile; and is an outbound client with no listening port. It also has an administrator — enterprise deployments get managed settings, an audit trail and a policy file, none of which the harness archetype has.
Against a sandboxed cloud execution service: the same agent run by the vendor on their infrastructure gets an isolated filesystem, default-deny egress and a clean teardown. Here it runs on a machine that also holds the developer's SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser profile, and nothing separates them from the agent's shell.

exemplars.name: Terminal and CLI coding agents
exemplars.note: Vendor agent loops that run in a shell against a working directory, with a permission model for file writes and command execution and support for project-scoped tool servers.

exemplars.name: IDE-embedded agents
exemplars.note: The same loop inside an editor, where the tool-server configuration lives in a dotfile in the repository. This is the specific location that has repeatedly proven to be a code-execution path when it can be written or swapped between approval and use.

exemplars.name: Managed enterprise deployments
exemplars.note: The same product with centrally managed settings, an allowlist of permitted tool servers and exported audit. The architecture is unchanged; the governance column is the difference.

zones.note: The developer, and everything the agent will read that someone else wrote.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Also holds the developer's SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions. Nothing in this archetype separates those from the agent's shell.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: Increasingly the default for command execution rather than an opt-in. Where it is present, it is the control that lets the approval gate fire rarely enough to be read.
zones.label: Isolated execution

zones.note: The inference API and, in managed deployments, the policy and audit endpoints.
zones.label: Provider · vendor service

zones.note: Remote tool providers the project depends on. Their behaviour belongs to the Agentic Platform persona; what remains controllable is whether they are admitted and how far they are scoped.
zones.label: Provider · third-party tools

zones.note: Present in managed deployments and absent otherwise. The same binary is a governed tool or an ungoverned one depending on whether this column exists.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Developer
nodes.note: Present, watching, and the approval gate. The archetype's posture depends on that staying true.

nodes.label: Repository content
nodes.note: Source files, dependency manifests, issue and PR text, build output. Contributed to by people who are not the developer, and read into context as though it were instruction.

nodes.label: Agent client
nodes.note: The terminal or editor the developer drives, and the vendor's loop behind it running as that developer. Outbound only — it accepts no connections, which is the single largest structural difference from a personal agent harness.

nodes.label: Planning loop
nodes.note: Decides the next edit or command from the task and everything it has read so far.

nodes.label: Agent configuration
nodes.note: The project file that declares which tool servers the agent may launch and what it is permitted to do without asking. It arrives with the repository, and it is the single most attacked artifact in this archetype — by injection into it, by modification after approval, and by auto-registration without a prompt.

nodes.label: Approval prompt
nodes.note: Blocks on writes and commands. Effective in inverse proportion to how often it fires: a prompt on every action is a click-through, so the surrounding controls exist to make it rare.

nodes.label: File and edit tools
nodes.note: Read and write across the working tree, and often beyond it. Scope is a setting, not a boundary.

nodes.label: Local tool servers
nodes.note: Child processes launched over stdio with the developer's privileges, admitted by the configuration file above.

nodes.label: Session credentials
nodes.note: Vendor-issued and session-scoped, which is the meaningful improvement over a long-lived key in a file. The developer's other credentials on the same machine are not.

nodes.label: Egress control
nodes.note: Default-deny outbound with an allowlist. The last boundary between a repository-borne injection and an attacker's collection endpoint.

nodes.label: Command execution
nodes.note: Builds, tests and shell commands. Isolating this is what turns "approve every command" into "approve the ones that leave the box".

nodes.label: Inference API
nodes.note: The published interface. What is behind it is the vendor's and is not drawn.

nodes.label: Remote tool servers
nodes.note: Third-party tool providers reached over HTTP. As OAuth resource servers they are a better trust story than a local child process — the grant is explicit, scoped and revocable — but their tool descriptions are still model input.

nodes.label: Managed settings
nodes.note: Centrally enforced permissions and a tool-server allowlist the developer cannot override. The difference between a governed deployment and a shadow one.

nodes.label: Session audit
nodes.note: Exported prompts, tool calls and approvals. Absent in unmanaged installs.

nodes.label: Shadow AI discovery
nodes.note: Finding the installs nobody registered, which on a developer machine is most of them.

control.note: Whoever is at the machine is the developer, as far as the agent is concerned.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Repository content is treated as untrusted on read. It cannot be authenticated — a contributor is not the developer — so the sandbox and the egress allowlist bound what a successful injection achieves.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: A tool server declared by a cloned repository is admitted only against a managed allowlist, never auto-registered. This is the specific crossing behind most of this archetype's disclosed code-execution paths.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: Two controls in series, and the reason the second can stay usable: with execution contained, only the actions that escape the box need a human.
control.title: Isolation boundary

control.note: Issued by the vendor per session and expiring on its own. The meaningful contrast with the personal-harness archetype, where the same authority sits in a file indefinitely.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Transport is authenticated; the content drives file writes and commands, and is not.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: An explicit grant to a named server, which is the strongest authentication on this diagram. It says nothing about whether the tool's own description is honest.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Tool output re-enters the context window. A compromised or merely hostile tool server writes directly into the agent's instructions.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Only meaningful if the enforcement is outside the file it governs. A policy stored beside the configuration it constrains is a suggestion.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: Which actions the developer is not permitted to auto-approve away.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: Present in managed deployments; in an unmanaged install there is no record at all.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: Finds the installs that never enrolled. Necessary precisely because this archetype is a binary a developer can fetch without asking anyone.
control.title: Independent discovery

crossCutting.note: The configuration file, the local servers it launches and the remote servers it names are one chain. Securing any single link leaves the path open, which is why the disclosed vulnerabilities in this archetype keep landing in different places along it.
Arrives through repository content, dependency metadata, tool output and test results — four unrelated paths into the same context window, none of which is the developer's instruction.
Everything in the governance column is optional. The same binary with no managed settings has no policy, no audit and no inventory, and that is the common case.

deviations.subject: The control plane is drawn even though most installs do not have one
deviations.reason: Unlike the personal-harness archetype, where no governance plane exists to draw, here it exists as a product feature and is simply not always deployed. Omitting it would hide the available answer; drawing it without saying so would overstate the typical posture. It is drawn, marked shared, and every node in it says what its absence means.

deviations.subject: Agent configuration is drawn as a registry node rather than a file
deviations.reason: Physically it is a dotfile. Functionally it is the admission decision for the entire tool plane, and the vocabulary's registry type is what carries that meaning. Drawing it as a data store would understate what writing to it achieves.

deviations.subject: Remote tool servers get their own vendor zone rather than sharing the vendor's
deviations.reason: They are a different third party with a different grant and a different failure mode. Folding them into the model vendor's boundary would imply one trust relationship where there are two.

archetypes.title: Desktop assistant with computer use
summary: A consumer-shaped desktop application that can read local files and drive the graphical interface — moving the pointer, typing, and clicking through applications that have no API and no concept of an agent operating them.
description:
Computer use is the distinguishing capability and the distinguishing problem. When an agent acts through the GUI it inherits every application already open and signed in, and it does so through an interface built entirely on the assumption that a human is driving. There is no authorization decision available at the point of action: the application receives a click.
This makes the archetype's authority impossible to scope with the usual tools. Tool permission scoping works when tools are named and enumerable; here the tool is "the screen", and the set of reachable actions is the set of things a person at that desk could do. The controls that remain are all about containment — running computer use inside a virtual machine with its own filesystem and its own signed-in accounts — and about the approval gate.
The input side is broad in a way the coding-agent archetype is not. A desktop assistant reads whatever the user points it at: documents, spreadsheets, screenshots, mail. Any of those may have been authored by someone else, and a screenshot in particular carries text the extraction step has no reliable way to classify. Screen content is model input with no provenance at all.
Connectors are the third axis. Desktop assistants increasingly hold standing grants into calendars, mail and file storage, authorised once through an OAuth flow the user completed in a moment of enthusiasm. Those grants outlive the task and are not scoped to it, which puts this archetype's real reach well beyond the machine it runs on.
distinguishedBy:
Against the agentic browser: that one's authority is a cookie jar and its input is a web page. This one's authority includes the local filesystem and every open desktop application, and its input includes screenshots — where an injection can be a picture of text.
Against the coding agent: same vendor discipline around credentials and updates, but no working directory to scope to and no repository to blame. The coding agent's blast radius is a project; this one's is a desktop.

exemplars.name: Desktop assistants with a computer-use mode
exemplars.note: A consumer application with local file access and an opt-in mode that drives the GUI, usually inside a contained virtual desktop rather than the user's own session.

exemplars.name: OS-integrated assistants
exemplars.note: Assistants shipped with the operating system, holding read access across local content and increasingly the ability to act in first-party applications.

zones.note: The user, and the documents and screens they point the assistant at.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: The assistant process, local files, and the user's own signed-in desktop session.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: A separate virtual desktop with its own filesystem and accounts, where computer use runs when the product offers it. The difference between a bounded blast radius and an unbounded one.
zones.label: Isolated execution

zones.note: Mail, calendar and storage the assistant holds standing OAuth grants into. Shared ownership because those grants are issued and revocable by each service, not by this device.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: Inference, and the connector broker behind the OAuth grants.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Device management, and whatever the vendor's administrative console exposes.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: User
nodes.note: Grants access, sets the task, and approves the actions the product decides to ask about.

nodes.label: Documents and screen content
nodes.note: Files, mail, spreadsheets and screenshots. A screenshot carries text with no provenance at all, which makes it the hardest input on this diagram to filter.

nodes.label: Assistant application
nodes.note: The window the user talks to, and where approvals appear.

nodes.label: Agent loop
nodes.note: Reads content, plans, and issues file operations or screen actions.

nodes.label: Local file access
nodes.note: Read and often write across the user's documents. Scoped by folder selection, which is a preference rather than an enforced boundary.

nodes.label: Action approval
nodes.note: The only authorization point available for GUI actions, because the applications being driven have none. Its coverage is a product decision.

nodes.label: Egress control
nodes.note: Where an exfiltration attempt is still stoppable after everything upstream has failed.

nodes.label: Screen and input control
nodes.note: Pointer, keyboard and screen capture. The tool that cannot be enumerated, because its reachable action set is everything visible.

nodes.label: Contained workspace
nodes.note: Files and sessions inside the container. What the agent can reach when containment is on, and the reason containment is the archetype's primary control.

nodes.label: Connected services
nodes.note: Standing grants into mail, calendar and storage. Authorised once, scoped to a service rather than a task, and outliving the conversation that prompted them.

nodes.label: Inference API
nodes.note: Receives document text and screenshots. The published interface; nothing behind it is drawn.

nodes.label: Device management
nodes.note: Whether the application may be installed, whether computer use may be enabled, and which folders it may reach.

nodes.label: Audit and detection
nodes.note: Endpoint telemetry plus whatever the vendor exports. Screen actions are the hardest thing on this diagram to reconstruct after the fact.

control.note: The consent that matters is granted once, in a dialog, and covers every future turn. It is the broadest authorization decision in the archetype and the least deliberated.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Documents and screen captures are classified on the way in. Screenshot text has no provenance at all, which is the hardest input on this diagram to filter.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: Carries documents and screenshots, which is usually more than the user pictured.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: The response drives a click on a real application. Its content is not authenticated.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Where computer use runs uncontained, this edge crosses into the user's own desktop instead and the boundary disappears entirely — leaving the approval prompt as the sole control.
control.title: Isolation boundary

control.note: Scoped to a service, not to a task or a turn. The grant that lets the assistant read one calendar invite lets it read the whole calendar, on every subsequent turn.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Mail and documents from connected services re-enter context. This is the same indirect injection path as retrieval, arriving through a grant the user forgot they gave.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: The only control here that does not depend on the assistant or the vendor behaving as described.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: Two partial views. Neither reliably reconstructs a sequence of screen actions, which is the archetype's weakest point for investigation.
control.title: Append-only audit

crossCutting.note: Driving a GUI means acting through interfaces with no authorization model. There is no node to attach the control to, because the applications being driven cannot tell an agent from a person — which is why containment rather than permission is the answer here.
Three unrelated inputs — local documents, screen pixels and connector content — reach the same context window, and the screenshot path has no provenance at all.
Standing connector grants plus broad local file access. Each was consented to individually; the reach is their union, and nobody consented to that.

deviations.subject: Screen and input control uses the browser-runtime node type
deviations.reason: The vocabulary has no computer-use type, and the browser runtime is the closest honest match: a driven interface carrying the user's existing authority, where every rendered surface is both input and action space. A dedicated type would be warranted if a second archetype needed it, and one does not yet.

deviations.subject: The contained desktop is drawn as a zone even where products run uncontained
deviations.reason: Containment is the archetype's primary control and the products that offer it make it the default. Drawing it always would overstate the field; omitting it would leave the strongest mitigation off the diagram. It is drawn, and the edge into it says what happens without it.

deviations.subject: Connected accounts are a zone rather than nodes inside the vendor boundary
deviations.reason: The grants are held by third-party services that are not the model vendor, and their revocation is controlled by neither the user's device nor the assistant. A separate zone with shared ownership is the only accurate placement.

archetypes.title: Local model runtime
summary: An open-weights model served on the user's own machine, listening on a local port so other applications can call it. Chosen to keep data off a vendor's infrastructure, which succeeds — and moves every control the vendor was providing onto the device.
description:
The reason people run this is sound: prompts and documents never leave the machine, there is no per-token cost, and it works offline. The architectural consequence is that the guardrails, rate limiting, abuse monitoring and content policy that a hosted API applies on the way in and out are simply absent. Nothing replaces them by default.
The runtime is a local network service. It binds a port, speaks an HTTP API, and historically ships without authentication because the assumed caller is a process on the same machine. That assumption fails in two directions: any local process — including a browser tab, through a permissive CORS policy — can call it, and a runtime bound to a routable interface rather than loopback is reachable from the network. This is the same exposure pattern as the personal agent harness, arrived at independently.
The supply chain is the second axis and the one specific to this archetype. Model weights are large binaries fetched from public hubs, and several serialization formats used to distribute them execute code on load. The format matters more than the source: a safe-by-construction tensor format from an unknown publisher is a better position than a pickle-based one from a known publisher. Scanning weights before they are loaded is the control, and the runtime is usually the thing that fetches them, so the scan has to sit in front of the fetch.
Worth stating plainly: this archetype removes a data-disclosure risk and adds a supply-chain and an exposure risk. Whether that is a good trade depends on which the organisation is actually managing, and the diagram is drawn so both sides are visible at once.
distinguishedBy:
Against self-hosted inference in a datacentre: identical software, entirely different operational reality. There the runtime has a network policy, an identity, a scanner in the pipeline and someone on call. Here it was installed by one person, has no inventory entry, and its port is protected by the assumption that nothing else on the machine is hostile.
Against the other endpoint archetypes: this one is not an agent. It has no loop, no tools and no autonomy — it is a dependency the others consume. It earns its own architecture because its risks are supply chain and local exposure rather than agency.

exemplars.name: Local inference servers
exemplars.note: Desktop applications and daemons that download open-weights models and expose an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API on a loopback port for other local software to call.

exemplars.name: OS and vendor-provided local runtimes
exemplars.note: Platform-level local inference offered as a system service, with a managed model catalogue. Narrower supply chain, same local-service exposure.

exemplars.name: Public model hubs
exemplars.note: Where the weights come from. Publisher identity is verifiable to varying degrees; what the artifact does on load is a property of its format, not its publisher.

zones.note: The model hub the weights come from, and anything else that can reach the machine.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: The runtime, the weights on disk, and the local applications that call it. One trust zone — any process here can reach the port.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: Everything a hosted API would have supplied, now the device owner's problem. Present only if someone put it there.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Public model hub
nodes.note: Distribution for open weights. Publisher identity ranges from verified to arbitrary, and the artifact's format decides whether loading it is an execution event.

nodes.label: Other local processes
nodes.note: Anything on the machine that can open a socket, including a browser tab where the runtime allows cross-origin requests. Not the caller the runtime was designed for.

nodes.label: Local HTTP API
nodes.note: An OpenAI-compatible endpoint on a loopback port. Frequently unauthenticated, because the assumed caller is trusted by virtue of being local — an assumption the browser breaks.

nodes.label: Inference runtime
nodes.note: Loads weights, batches requests, serves completions. Also the process that fetches the weights, which is why the supply-chain control has to sit in front of it.

nodes.label: Loaded model
nodes.note: Open weights running with no provider-side guardrail, no abuse monitoring and no content policy. Whatever safety behaviour exists is whatever the weights carry.

nodes.label: Weights on disk
nodes.note: Multi-gigabyte artifacts. Their format determines whether loading them is deserialization or execution, and that is a more useful question than who published them.

nodes.label: Local guardrails
nodes.note: Input and output classification, if anyone deployed it. Drawn because its absence is the archetype's defining property and a diagram without it has nowhere to say so.

nodes.label: Model inventory
nodes.note: Which models are on which machines, at which versions, from which source. Almost never exists, and is the precondition for responding to a bad model release.

nodes.label: Weight scanning
nodes.note: Format and content inspection before load. The one control that addresses the archetype's distinctive risk rather than a borrowed one.

nodes.label: Runtime policy
nodes.note: Whether local inference is permitted at all, from which sources, and bound to which interface.

control.note: Transport is authenticated and the publisher may be verifiable. Neither says anything about what the artifact does when the runtime opens it.
control.title: Verified provenance

control.note: The local API authenticates its callers rather than treating locality as authorisation. That assumption is what a browser tab breaks through a permissive cross-origin policy.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Only a control if it runs before the runtime opens the file. A scan that reports after the fact has documented an incident rather than prevented one.
control.title: Artifact integrity

control.note: Derived from what is installed rather than from anything the runtime reports, because an unregistered runtime is exactly the one worth finding.
control.title: Independent discovery

control.note: Loopback-only binding, enforced by the device rather than requested of the application. This is the control that closes the exposure path.
control.title: Tenant configuration

crossCutting.note: Spans the hub, the file and the loader. No single node owns it: it is a property of the artifact format travelling across all three, which is why format policy beats source policy.
This archetype is installed by one person in an afternoon and appears in no inventory. Every governance control listed here presumes someone knows the runtime exists.
No provider-side safety layer anywhere in the diagram. Whatever the weights do is the whole of the behaviour, and the consumer applications were built expecting a hosted API's floor.

deviations.subject: Local guardrails are drawn although most installs have none
deviations.reason: Their absence is the point of the archetype, and a diagram cannot show an absence without first having a place for the thing. Drawn inline with a note saying it is optional, which states the position more clearly than leaving a gap in the flow.

deviations.subject: Other local processes are drawn as an untrusted actor
deviations.reason: They are on the same device, which normally implies the same trust zone. They are drawn outside it because the runtime's authentication model treats locality as authorization, and naming that assumption as a boundary is the only way to show it failing.

deviations.subject: There is no vendor zone
deviations.reason: Removing it is the entire reason this architecture is chosen. Its absence is what shifts guardrails, rate limiting and abuse monitoring onto the device owner, and the diagram should be read as the vendor column having moved into the governance one.

archetypes.title: Local MCP and tool plane
summary: The fleet of tool servers running on a developer's machine and the configuration files that admit them. Not an agent — the substrate every local agent shares, and the place where this surface's disclosed vulnerabilities have concentrated.
description:
Every endpoint agent archetype in this catalogue reads a configuration file to decide which tool servers to launch and what they may do without asking. Those files are the admission decision for the whole tool plane, and they are ordinary files: writable by the user, writable by anything running as the user, and frequently committed to the repository they configure.
Three distinct failure modes have shown up repeatedly, and they are worth separating because they need different controls. Injection into the file adds a server nobody approved. Swapping the file after approval means the thing that was reviewed is not the thing that runs, which is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use problem and not an access-control one. Auto-registration means a server is admitted with no approval step at all. Only the second is fixed by integrity checking; the first needs write protection and the third needs the product to stop doing it.
A local server is a child process with the user's privileges. There is no sandbox between it and the filesystem, no scope on what it may read, and no identity distinguishing it from the agent that launched it. The protocol's authorization work is aimed at remote servers, where there is a boundary to authorize across; over stdio there is nothing to authenticate to.
Tool descriptions are model input. A server declares what its tools do in text the agent reads and acts on, which means a hostile server does not need a vulnerability — it can simply describe itself persuasively. Servers also change their descriptions between calls, so a description approved once is not the description used later.
The last piece is accumulation. Servers get added for one task and never removed, and their grants persist. An inventory of what is admitted, on which machines, with which scopes is the control that makes the rest possible, and it is the one least often present.
distinguishedBy:
Against the agent archetypes that use it: those describe a loop and its authority. This describes the admission mechanism they all share. It is drawn separately because the vulnerabilities land here rather than in any one agent, and because fixing it fixes all of them.
Against a remote MCP server you publish: that is a service with an OAuth boundary, an operator and a tenancy model. This is a child process with your privileges and no boundary at all. They share a protocol and almost nothing else.

exemplars.name: Project-scoped tool configuration files
exemplars.note: Dotfiles in a repository declaring which tool servers an agent should launch. Ship with the clone, and have been the specific location of multiple disclosed code-execution paths.

exemplars.name: User-scoped and managed tool configuration
exemplars.note: The same declaration at user or device level. Managed variants let an administrator pin an allowlist the user cannot override, which is the only durable fix for auto-registration.

exemplars.name: Community tool servers
exemplars.note: Servers installed from package registries and run as child processes. Reviewed by whoever installed them, updated automatically, and holding the user's full privileges.

zones.note: Package registries, repositories, and the remote services some servers front.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Agent, configuration and servers all run as the same user in one trust zone. There is no internal boundary to draw because there is none to have.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: Allowlisting, integrity checking and inventory. Available in managed deployments, absent by default, and the difference between the two is the whole of this archetype's posture.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Package registry
nodes.note: Where servers are installed from and updated. Publisher identity is verifiable; behaviour is not, and behaviour changes on update.

nodes.label: Repository-supplied config
nodes.note: A tool-server declaration that arrived with a clone. Authored by whoever last committed to the project, and read on the next agent start.

nodes.label: Agent client
nodes.note: Whichever agent is consuming the plane. Interchangeable — the point of drawing this separately is that the plane outlives and is shared by all of them.

nodes.label: Tool configuration
nodes.note: The admission decision: which servers launch, and what runs without a prompt. In the target state it is write-protected from the plane it governs — left as an ordinary user-writable file, a compromised server can add its own successor, which is the loop that turns one bad package into a persistent foothold.

nodes.label: Server approval
nodes.note: Shown on first use of a server. Approves what the file said at that moment, which is not necessarily what it says when the server is next launched.

nodes.label: Local tool servers
nodes.note: Child processes over stdio, holding the user's privileges. No sandbox, no scope, no identity of their own, and nothing to authenticate to.

nodes.label: Tool descriptions
nodes.note: What each server tells the model its tools do. Model input, author-controlled, and re-read on each connection — so an approved description is not a durable fact.

nodes.label: Server credentials
nodes.note: API tokens the servers need for the services they front, typically in environment variables or the config file itself — readable by every other server in the plane.

nodes.label: Server allowlist
nodes.note: Which servers may be admitted, enforced outside the file being governed. The only durable answer to auto-registration.

nodes.label: Config integrity
nodes.note: Detects the file changing between approval and launch. Addresses the time-of-check problem specifically, which access control does not.

nodes.label: Tool plane inventory
nodes.note: Which servers are admitted on which machines with which scopes. Servers accumulate and are never removed, so without this the plane only grows.

control.note: Publisher identity at publish time, nothing at launch time. An update changes the code running with the user's privileges without any further decision.
control.title: Verified provenance

control.note: Project-supplied tool declarations are proposals, admitted against an allowlist enforced outside the file. Auto-registration is the failure this replaces.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: The target state runs local servers with their own filesystem and network policy rather than as child processes holding the user's privileges. Nothing in the protocol provides this; the client has to.
control.title: Isolation boundary

control.note: Has to live somewhere the plane cannot reach. An allowlist stored beside the file it governs shares that file's threat model.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: Catches the swap between approval and launch, which is the failure integrity checking exists for.
control.title: Artifact integrity

control.note: Derived from the machine, not self-reported, because the unregistered server is the one that matters.
control.title: Independent discovery

crossCutting.note: Three separate paths reach it — repository-supplied config, a server writing to the file that admitted it, and swapping the file between approval and launch. They need three different controls, which is why patching one keeps producing another disclosure.
Servers are added per task and removed never. The accumulated plane is nobody's decision; it is the sum of a year of individually reasonable ones.
Every server in the plane can read every other server's environment. Isolation between them is a property nothing in this archetype provides.

deviations.subject: This is drawn as an archetype although it is not an application
deviations.reason: It is a substrate the agent archetypes share rather than something anyone deploys on its own. It earns a diagram because the disclosed vulnerabilities on this surface cluster here rather than in any one agent, and because a reader who fixes this fixes all of them at once. The alternative — repeating the tool plane inside every endpoint archetype — would state it four times and improve none of them.

deviations.subject: A server writing to its own admission file is not drawn
deviations.reason: An earlier draft drew it, because it is the loop that turns one compromised package into a persistent foothold. It is not drawn now because these are target architectures: in the state being described the configuration is write-protected from the plane it governs, so the edge does not exist. The point survives on the configuration node and in its risks, which is where a property of a component belongs rather than as a flow nobody should build.

deviations.subject: No sandbox zone is drawn
deviations.reason: Local servers over stdio are not sandboxed by any current implementation, and drawing an empty container would imply an option that does not exist here. Where execution is contained, it is contained by the consuming agent, and that is drawn in the coding-agent archetype.

archetypes.title: Personal autonomous agent harness
summary: An always-on daemon on a personal device that takes ambient messages from anyone who can reach its channels, runs an unattended agent loop with the user's own credentials, and keeps what it learns in files it will read back as instruction.
description:
The harness is a long-lived process, not an invocation. It owns a gateway that binds a local port, one bridge per messaging channel, an agent loop, a set of tools that run as the user, and a memory directory. Nothing about it is scoped to a task: it starts when the machine starts and ends when the user kills it.
Three properties in combination make this a distinct architecture rather than a variation on a coding assistant, and every one of them is visible in the diagram.
It listens. A gateway on a local port with channel bridges attached is a network service. Whoever can reach a bridge can address the agent, and the bridge — not the model — is the authorization decision. Bridges are also where the authorization bugs concentrate, because each new channel is a separate implementation of the same admission check.
It runs unattended. A scheduled tick starts the loop with nobody watching, so there is no moment at which a human sees the plan before the tools execute.
It remembers in a medium it re-reads as instruction. Memory is prose the next turn treats as context. A single successful injection that writes to the memory or heartbeat file survives restarts and re-executes on the schedule, which is a persistence mechanism with an indistinguishable footprint from normal operation.
The skill supply chain is the second structural weakness. Skills combine prose and executable code in one artifact and load into the agent's own process, so a skill is not a plugin with an API surface — it is code running with the agent's full authority, admitted on the strength of a publisher's own description. Scanners that read declared behaviour rather than observed behaviour have been bypassed repeatedly, across several independent registries.
What the diagram does not contain is the point. There is no management zone: no identity for the agent distinct from the user, no policy engine consulted per tool call, no audit sink, no registry deciding what may be installed, no kill switch beyond killing the process. Credentials sit at rest inside the same blast radius as the code that reads them. Every governance control in this repository's taxonomy that applies here has to be brought by the endpoint, because the architecture supplies none of it.
distinguishedBy:
Against a vendor coding agent: the coding agent is invoked by a human who is present, reads content the user chose, holds session-scoped credentials issued by a vendor, and is an outbound client. The harness is triggered by strangers and by a timer, reads whatever arrives, holds long-lived keys the user pasted in, and listens on a port. Nobody has ever found a hundred thousand exposed coding agents, because a coding agent does not accept connections.
Against a cloud agent service: the same loop hosted by a provider gets an identity, a policy boundary, an audit trail and an administrator by default. Moving this architecture off the endpoint changes almost nothing about the loop and almost everything about the governance.

exemplars.name: OpenClaw
exemplars.note: The reference implementation of the pattern and the origin of most public evidence about it: a Node gateway daemon owning all state, channel bridges for a dozen messaging platforms, an embedded agent runtime, Markdown memory with a scheduled heartbeat, in-process skills from a public registry, and paired device nodes exposing camera, screen and remote execution.

exemplars.name: Hermes Agent
exemplars.note: An independent implementation with a more mature posture and an unusually candid threat model, which states plainly that its deny rules guard against an honest-but-wrong agent rather than an adversarial one. Its self-improvement feature — the agent writing its own skills — is the persistence vector in this archetype made into a product decision.

exemplars.name: Homegrown harnesses
exemplars.note: The long tail: a script, a messaging webhook, an API key in a dotfile, and cron. Structurally identical and considerably more common than either named project.

zones.note: Everything that can address the agent or be read by it. The senders are not a subset of the user's contacts, and the content is not a subset of what the user chose to open.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: One trust zone containing the daemon, its tools, its memory, and its credentials. There is no internal boundary: a tool that runs here can read the memory files and the key file.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: Isolation exists as an option and is typically not the default. Where it is enabled, its configuration is itself reachable by the agent unless the host prevents it, which has been the subject of more than one sandbox-escape finding.
zones.label: Isolated execution

zones.note: The inference API. Reached directly from the device over a key the user holds.
zones.label: Provider

nodes.label: Owner
nodes.note: The person the agent acts for, addressing it over the same channels as everyone else.

nodes.label: Unsolicited senders
nodes.note: Anyone who can reach a connected channel. On a public messaging network that is an unbounded set, and the message body is model input.

nodes.label: Fetched content
nodes.note: Pages, documents and API responses the tools retrieve. Attacker-writable, and it re-enters the loop as context indistinguishable from the user's own words.

nodes.label: Public skill registry
nodes.note: An open marketplace of prose-plus-code extensions. Admission is publisher self-attestation; the declared behaviour of a package and its actual behaviour are separate facts.

nodes.label: Channel bridges
nodes.note: One adapter per messaging platform, each implementing its own sender check. The count of channels is the count of independent authorization surfaces, which is why the disclosed authorization bypasses in this archetype cluster in newly added bridges.

nodes.label: Heartbeat
nodes.note: A periodic tick that starts the loop with no human present and re-reads the memory files. The mechanism that converts a one-time injection into a recurring one.

nodes.label: Gateway daemon
nodes.note: One long-lived process: the gateway that owns every piece of state and binds a local port, and the loop that plans, calls tools and reads the results back as context. Historically bound to all interfaces, which is how exposure scans found instances by the tens of thousands; current builds bind loopback with authentication.

nodes.label: Memory and index
nodes.note: Cross-session, cross-conversation, plain-text files plus the embedded search over them. Written by the agent, read back as instruction on every subsequent turn including the unattended ones. This is the persistence primitive.

nodes.label: Installed skills
nodes.note: Prose and executable code from the registry, loaded into the daemon's own process. Not sandboxed from the agent by construction — a skill has whatever the agent has.

nodes.label: Shell and file tools
nodes.note: Command execution and filesystem access running as the user. The authority here is the user account, not a scoped grant, so the reachable set is everything the user can reach.

nodes.label: Local MCP servers
nodes.note: Tool providers launched as child processes over stdio. Admission is a config file the agent can usually write, which makes tool registration a self-service operation for anything that has already achieved code execution.

nodes.label: Paired device nodes
nodes.note: Companion devices exposing camera, screen, location and remote execution to the same loop. Extends the blast radius from one machine to the user's physical surroundings.

nodes.label: API keys at rest
nodes.note: Long-lived provider keys and channel tokens in a config file the agent's own tools can read. A store, not a broker: the same secret every time, revocable only by hand.

nodes.label: Response rendering
nodes.note: Replies back onto the channel, and anywhere else the agent decides to send them.

nodes.label: Sandboxed execution
nodes.note: Where code execution goes when isolation is turned on. Worth drawing precisely because it is optional: the same diagram without this zone is the common deployment.

nodes.label: Inference API
nodes.note: The published interface. Everything behind it is the provider's, and is not drawn.

control.note: The bridge decides the sender is the owner from the messaging platform's own identifier. That identifier is as strong as the platform makes it, and the agent has no second factor.
control.title: User identity

control.note: An allowlist of permitted senders, enforced once for every bridge rather than configured per bridge. Without it any party who can reach a channel can address the agent.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: No signature the runtime verifies against a trusted root, and no admission decision by anyone but the installing user. Review has to cover prose and code in the same artifact.
control.title: Verified provenance

control.note: Fetched content is classified before it re-enters context. The primary injection path once the agent is running, and the reason the egress allowlist matters as much as the filter.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: A bearer token from the local key file, unscoped to the request and typically valid until someone notices. Anything that can read the file inherits the account.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Transport is authenticated; the content of the response is not, and it drives tool calls.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: A device pairs once and stays paired. The grant is to the harness, so it is also a grant to anything that has compromised the harness.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Only present when isolation is enabled. Where the agent can also reach the container's own configuration, the boundary is advisory.
control.title: Isolation boundary

control.note: Replies go wherever the agent addresses them, which is not necessarily back to the sender who prompted the turn — a covert-channel path worth naming.
control.title: Authenticated transport

crossCutting.note: The harness, its bridges, its skills and its MCP servers are all third-party code in one process. No single node owns this; the whole device zone is one dependency surface.
Nothing in the architecture registers the agent with anyone. An organisation discovers these by scanning for them, which is a property of the archetype rather than of any component.
Unattended triggering, unscoped tool authority and no approval gate compound. Each is survivable alone; the combination is what makes a single injection consequential.

deviations.subject: No management zone is drawn
deviations.reason: This archetype has no governance plane, and inventing one would misrepresent it. There is no agent identity distinct from the user, no per-call policy decision, no audit sink, no admission registry and no kill switch beyond terminating the process. The governance capabilities listed above are all things an organisation must impose from the endpoint; none is supplied by the architecture. The empty column is the finding.

deviations.subject: The optional container is drawn as a zone rather than omitted
deviations.reason: Isolation is available in every mature implementation and enabled in a minority of deployments. Drawing it always would overstate the typical posture; omitting it would hide the single most effective structural mitigation. It is drawn, and its note says it is opt-in.

deviations.subject: Paired device nodes are modelled as an actuator rather than their own zone
deviations.reason: A paired phone is a second device with its own trust boundary, and a fuller treatment would give it a zone. It is drawn as one node here because the security-relevant fact is the grant from the harness, not the companion device's internal structure.
