archetypes.title: Enterprise AI chat with connectors
summary: A general-purpose assistant subscription for the workforce, where each user connects their own data sources. The grant model is per user and per connector, which makes the organisation's total exposure a sum nobody computes.
description:
The contrast with a tenant-wide assistant is entirely in who consents. There, an administrator grants the vendor access to the corpus once and the assistant inherits each user's entitlements against it. Here, each user authorises their own connectors — a repository, a drive, a ticket system — and the organisation's data path to the vendor is the union of thousands of individual decisions, each made in a modal dialog.
This makes the archetype's core problem visibility rather than permission. Any single grant is usually appropriate: a person connecting a system they already have access to has not escalated anything. What nobody has is the aggregate — which systems are connected, by how many people, carrying what classification — and no individual is positioned to notice when the sum becomes a problem.
File upload is the parallel path and often the larger one. A user pasting a document into a chat window has moved data across the boundary with no connector, no grant and no record beyond what network inspection catches. Every control that watches connectors misses this entirely, which is why in-browser and network inspection carry more weight in this archetype than the vendor's own administrative surface does.
The remaining structural question is the boundary between the enterprise tenant and the consumer product. The same vendor typically offers both, the consumer one has different retention and training terms, and the difference between a user being in your tenant and being signed into their own account is a session cookie. Detecting and blocking the consumer variant is a distinct control from governing the enterprise one, and it is usually the one that matters more.
distinguishedBy:
Against the tenant-wide assistant: administrator-granted and corpus-wide there, user-granted and connector-by-connector here. That single difference relocates the entire control set from permissions governance to discovery and aggregate visibility.
Against shadow AI: this is the sanctioned version of the same traffic. Drawing them separately is deliberate — the sanctioned tenant is where you want the traffic to go, and most of the work in this archetype is about making sure it does.

exemplars.name: Enterprise assistant subscriptions
exemplars.note: Workforce-wide licences for a general assistant, with administrative controls over retention, training and which connectors may be enabled.

exemplars.name: Per-user connector catalogues
exemplars.note: Marketplaces of source connectors each user authorises for themselves, typically over OAuth, with the vendor holding the resulting grant.

zones.note: The consumer version of the same product, and content that arrives through connectors.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Where uploads happen and where the difference between the corporate tenant and a personal account is visible. The most important vantage point in this archetype.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: Which tenant traffic reaches, and what leaves with it.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: Systems the Data Provider persona is responsible for, reached by grants individual AI System Users issued.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: Inference, conversation storage and the connector broker.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Tenant configuration the Governance persona authors, plus the discovery and inspection it runs independently of the vendor.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Consumer product
nodes.note: The same vendor's unmanaged offering, reachable from the same browser with a personal login. Different retention terms, no administrative visibility, one cookie away.

nodes.label: Content from connected systems
nodes.note: Tickets, documents and messages retrieved through a connector, authored by people outside the conversation and entering it as context.

nodes.label: Employee
nodes.note: Authorises their own connectors and uploads their own files. Every grant reasonable, the aggregate visible to nobody.

nodes.label: Chat surface
nodes.note: Browser tab or desktop client. The last point where the prompt, the attachment and the tenant it is going to are all visible to something the organisation operates.

nodes.label: File upload
nodes.note: The path that no connector governance sees. A pasted document crosses the boundary with no grant, no scope and no record other than what inspection catches.

nodes.label: Identity provider
nodes.note: Establishes the user and, critically, which tenant they are in. Tenant restriction enforced here is what stops the consumer product being an alternative.

nodes.label: Secure service edge
nodes.note: Inline inspection and tenant enforcement. Does most of the real work in this archetype because the vendor's admin console cannot see the traffic that never reached the managed tenant.

nodes.label: User-connected systems
nodes.note: Repositories, drives and trackers, each authorised by an individual. Their union is the organisation's actual data path to the vendor.

nodes.label: Tenant API
nodes.note: The published interface. Inference, storage and the connector broker are behind it.

nodes.label: Connector broker
nodes.note: Holds the OAuth grants users issued and calls their systems on their behalf. The grants persist after the conversation, after the project, and after the employee.

nodes.label: Tenant configuration
nodes.note: Retention, training opt-out, which connectors are permitted, and whether conversation history is exportable. Set once and rarely revisited against a product that ships new connectors.

nodes.label: Connector inventory
nodes.note: Which sources are connected, by how many people, holding what classification. The aggregate no individual grant decision produces.

nodes.label: Shadow AI discovery
nodes.note: Finding traffic to the consumer product and to competing tools. Usually surfaces more data movement than the sanctioned tenant does.

nodes.label: Audit and detection
nodes.note: Vendor export plus first-party network and browser telemetry. The second is the part that covers uploads and the consumer tenant.

control.note: The only control on this path. Connector governance does not see uploads, and the vendor's admin console sees them only after they have arrived.
control.title: Device posture and inspection

control.note: The prompt itself is inspected here or nowhere. Once it reaches the vendor, only the vendor can see it, and only at the fidelity their export offers.
control.title: Device posture and inspection

control.note: Asserting which tenant a user may reach is what makes the sanctioned product the only available one. Without it the consumer version is a login away.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Authenticates the user into the managed tenant, where retention and training terms apply. Everything the enterprise agreement promises depends on the traffic arriving here.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Where inspection is absent this crossing simply succeeds, and none of the enterprise terms apply to anything that goes through it.
control.title: Egress allowlist

control.note: A per-user grant, made in a dialog, scoped to a whole system rather than a task, and outliving the conversation that prompted it. Reasonable individually; the aggregate is the organisation's data path.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Acts as the user who consented. Correct as far as access control goes, and invisible to anyone trying to see the total.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Content authored elsewhere enters the conversation as context. The same indirect injection path as retrieval, arriving through a grant one employee made.
control.title: Provider-internal

control.note: Response content is not authenticated, and is rendered into a browser.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Authored by the Governance persona, enforced by the provider, unverifiable by either. Worth re-reviewing whenever the vendor ships a connector, because the default for new ones is rarely off.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: The only way to see the aggregate, and it depends on the vendor exposing per-user grants to an administrator.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: Independent of the vendor, which is the point — it finds the tenants nobody enrolled.
control.title: Independent discovery

control.note: Covers uploads and the consumer tenant, neither of which appears in any vendor export.
control.title: Append-only audit

crossCutting.note: Produced by summation, not by any decision. Thousands of individually appropriate consents whose union nobody computed and no single user could have.
The consumer version of the same product is one login away and carries none of the enterprise terms. The sanctioned tenant's governance is only as good as the enforcement that traffic reaches it.
Two paths — connectors and uploads — with completely different control sets. Governing the first and ignoring the second is the common failure.

deviations.subject: The vendor's consumer product is drawn in the outside world
deviations.reason: It is the same vendor and often the same interface, so drawing it inside the vendor zone would be defensible. It is drawn outside because its terms, its retention and its visibility are those of an unmanaged third party, and the tenant boundary — not the vendor boundary — is what actually governs the data.

deviations.subject: File upload is drawn as a connector node on the device
deviations.reason: It is not an integration and has no grant, which is exactly why it needs to be on the diagram. Giving it a node forces the question of what watches it, and the answer is a different control set from the one governing connectors.

deviations.subject: Individual user grants are drawn as one edge
deviations.reason: There are thousands, made independently. Drawing one and naming the aggregation problem in its note is more truthful than a diagram that implies a single administrative decision.

archetypes.title: Vendor low-code agent builder
summary: A vendor platform where non-engineers assemble agents from prompts, connectors and triggers. The agents are real, the authors are not engineers, and there is no code review between an afternoon's work and something that acts on production data.
description:
Everything that makes this category valuable is also what makes it distinct as an architecture: the builder is a self-service surface. A business user can create an agent, grant it connectors, give it a trigger and publish it to colleagues, without any of the checkpoints a software delivery pipeline would impose. There is no pull request, no review, no staged rollout and no security sign-off unless the platform enforces one.
The result is a population problem rather than an instance problem. Individual agents are usually simple; the risk is that there are four hundred of them, each with connector grants, each authored by someone who has left, and no one can list which reach customer data. Every control in this archetype is therefore about the population — an inventory, a publication gate, an environment boundary between draft and shared, and a way to revoke a class of grant.
Credential inheritance is the specific technical trap. A low-code agent typically runs on connections authorised by its author, so a published agent acts with its author's access for every colleague who uses it. A user who could not read a table directly can often read it through an agent someone else built, and neither party intended that. Whether the platform supports per-invoker authorization rather than author-credential execution is the single question worth asking during evaluation.
The authoring surface is also an injection surface. Instructions, knowledge sources and connector descriptions are assembled by someone who is not thinking about untrusted input, and a shared agent's knowledge source is frequently a folder anyone can write to.
distinguishedBy:
Against the vendor action agent: that is one agent the vendor built and you configured. This is a platform on which your own people build many, and the unit of concern moves from the configuration of one to the governance of a population.
Against an internal AI platform you operate: same intent — a paved road for many builders — with the paving done by a vendor. You inherit their guardrails and their environment model, and you cannot add a deployment gate they did not build.

exemplars.name: Suite-embedded agent builders
exemplars.note: Low-code agent authoring bundled with a productivity or CRM suite, available to any licensed user by default unless an administrator turns it off.

exemplars.name: Standalone agent-building platforms
exemplars.note: Vendor platforms whose product is the builder itself, with connector marketplaces and publication to internal or external audiences.

zones.note: Whoever ends up talking to a published agent, and whoever wrote its knowledge sources.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Business users authoring agents, and colleagues consuming them. Not engineers, and not operating under an engineering process.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: Who is authenticated, and whose credentials an agent ends up running on.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: The systems the connectors reach. Reached by agents nobody reviewed.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: Authoring, hosting and execution of the agents. The Governance persona decides who may use it, not how it runs.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Population management: who may build, what may be published, what is connected, and what can be revoked at once.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Agent consumers
nodes.note: Colleagues, and sometimes customers, using an agent built by someone else. Rarely aware of whose credentials it runs on.

nodes.label: Attached knowledge sources
nodes.note: Folders, sites and documents attached to an agent as grounding. Often writable by more people than the agent's audience, which turns a shared drive into an instruction channel.

nodes.label: Citizen builder
nodes.note: Authors the instructions, attaches the connectors, and publishes. Not operating under code review, and frequently no longer at the company by the time the agent matters.

nodes.label: Authoring surface
nodes.note: Prompt, connectors, triggers, publication. Every one of those is a security decision made by someone who was not asked to make one.

nodes.label: Identity provider
nodes.note: Authenticates builders and consumers. Whether the consumer's identity — rather than the author's — reaches the connector is the archetype's decisive question.

nodes.label: Connected systems
nodes.note: Whatever the connectors reach. The union across all published agents is the platform's real data footprint, and no single agent's author can see it.

nodes.label: Agent runtime
nodes.note: The published interface. Authoring, hosting and execution behind it are the vendor's.

nodes.label: Connector framework
nodes.note: The vendor's integration layer. Its authorization model — author credentials or invoker credentials — decides whether publishing an agent is also a privilege grant.

nodes.label: Agent inventory
nodes.note: Every agent, its author, its connectors, its audience and its last use. The one control that makes the population tractable, and the one most platforms report on rather than enforce.

nodes.label: Publication gate
nodes.note: Review before an agent reaches an audience beyond its author. The nearest available thing to code review, and it exists only if the platform offers it and an administrator turned it on.

nodes.label: Environment and connector policy
nodes.note: Which connectors may be combined, which environments allow publication, and who may build at all. Blocking a connector pairing is more tractable than reviewing every agent.

nodes.label: Usage audit
nodes.note: Which agents ran, for whom, reaching what. The basis for retiring the ones nobody uses.

control.note: Building an agent typically requires no elevated role. The permission to create something that acts on company data is the same permission as opening a document.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Authenticates the author. Says nothing about whether anyone reviewed what they wrote.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Authenticates the consumer to the platform. Whether that identity continues to the connector, or is replaced by the author's, is the difference between an access-control system that works and one that is bypassed by publishing.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Whoever can write to the attached folder can write instructions the agent will follow for every one of its users.
control.title: Existing content permissions

control.note: Not observable. The decision and the call both happen inside the vendor boundary.
control.title: Provider-internal

control.note: The archetype's decisive crossing. Author-delegated means a published agent lends the author's access to everyone who uses it; invoker-delegated preserves the access model the organisation already has.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Also where building can be restricted to a licensed subset, which is the bluntest and often most effective population control available.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Preventing a combination — a source of confidential data plus a path to send mail — scales where reviewing individual agents does not.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: Only covers publication, not creation. A private agent with production connectors is outside its scope and inside the risk.
control.title: Human approval

control.note: Reported by the platform rather than discovered independently. Adequate here, because unlike a local install there is no way to build an agent off-platform.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: Vendor-shaped, and the basis for retiring agents nobody has used in a year.
control.title: Append-only audit

crossCutting.note: Not a property of any agent. It is what happens when creation is self-service and retirement is nobody's job, and it is the reason every control here is a population control.
Whether an agent runs as its author or its invoker determines whether publishing is also a privilege grant. One platform setting, and it decides whether the access model holds.
Each connector grant is defensible alone. The union across hundreds of agents authored by people who never met is nobody's decision and nobody's picture.

deviations.subject: One diagram stands for a population of agents
deviations.reason: The platform hosts hundreds of agents and the diagram shows one path through it. That is the right abstraction here: the individual agents are simple and near-identical in structure, and everything that makes the archetype hard is in the governance column, which is drawn per population rather than per agent.

deviations.subject: The builder is drawn as a node inside a trust zone rather than a boundary actor
deviations.reason: They are your own staff, inside your perimeter. They are drawn as a node because in this archetype the author is a component of the system — their credentials frequently execute it — rather than a party who merely uses it.

deviations.subject: No sandbox or runtime enforcement appears
deviations.reason: Neither is available. You cannot insert a policy decision point into a vendor's agent loop, and the capability taxonomy records that as structurally unavailable on this surface. The controls that remain are admission, connector scoping and inventory, and those are what is drawn.

archetypes.title: Shadow AI services and extensions
summary: AI services in use that nobody sanctioned: consumer accounts on enterprise-grade tools, browser extensions with page access, and API keys expensed to a team card. Not a design — a discovered architecture, and the one most organisations actually have.
description:
This archetype is drawn because the alternative is pretending it does not exist. Every other architecture in this catalogue assumes someone decided to build or buy it. This one assembles itself from individually reasonable choices: a person with a deadline, a free tier, and a browser. The diagram is what the environment already looks like before any governance programme reaches it.
Three distinct paths carry data out, and they need different detection. A consumer account on a web service moves data through the browser under a personal login. A browser extension with host permissions reads pages continuously with no login at all. A direct API key on a corporate card moves data from a server or a script, never touches a browser, and shows up in expense data long before it shows up in network logs.
The Governance persona's problem is that discovery is the whole control. There is no configuration to harden and no vendor to negotiate with, because the relationship was never formed. Every downstream control — DLP, tenant enforcement, contractual terms — presupposes knowing the service is in use, and the discovery signals are network telemetry, browser inventory, identity logs and expense records, which sit in four different systems owned by three different teams.
The outcome that matters is not blocking. Blocking a service without providing a sanctioned equivalent moves the traffic to a service that is harder to see. The productive path is discovery, then a sanctioned tenant of the same class of tool, then enforcement that makes the sanctioned path the easy one — which is why this archetype's natural terminus is the enterprise chat archetype, and why they are drawn as a pair.
distinguishedBy:
Against the enterprise AI chat archetype: the same traffic, on the wrong side of every control. That one has a tenant, terms, an admin console and an audit export. This one has none, and the work is finding it rather than configuring it.
Against every other archetype here: those describe systems someone designed. This one describes what is discovered, and it is the only diagram in the catalogue where the governance column is the entire architecture rather than a plane beside it.

exemplars.name: Consumer accounts on enterprise tools
exemplars.note: A personal login to the same vendor the organisation may already pay for, with consumer retention and training terms and no administrative visibility.

exemplars.name: AI browser extensions
exemplars.note: Extensions requesting host permissions across all sites, installed in one click and updated silently. Reads pages continuously rather than when invoked.

exemplars.name: Direct API keys on expense
exemplars.note: A provider key paid for on a team card and used from a script or a server. Invisible to browser controls and usually the largest single data volume of the three.

zones.note: Providers with no contract, no tenant configuration and no relationship. Not adversaries — simply parties nobody agreed terms with.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Where all three paths begin, and the only place two of them are observable. Device and browser telemetry does most of the work in this archetype.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: The vantage point that sees destinations regardless of which path the data took.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: Servers and scripts calling provider APIs directly. The path with no browser in it, and therefore no browser control on it.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: In this archetype the control plane is the architecture. Everything else on the diagram is what it is trying to find.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Consumer AI service

nodes.label: Extension distribution
nodes.note: Install and silent update for extensions holding page-read permissions. A supply chain with no enrolment step.

nodes.label: Provider API
nodes.note: A model API reached with a key nobody registered. The highest-volume path and the least visible to anything watching browsers.

nodes.label: Employee
nodes.note: Solving a real problem with the tool that was available. Treating this as misconduct rather than as unmet demand is what pushes the next attempt somewhere harder to see.

nodes.label: Browser
nodes.note: Carries two of the three paths — the consumer login and the extension. The single most valuable place to instrument on this diagram.

nodes.label: Installed extension
nodes.note: Reads pages whether or not it is being used. Its permission grant was one click and its updates need none.

nodes.label: Secure service edge
nodes.note: Sees destinations for every path, and content for the ones where inspection is terminated. The backstop when device controls are absent or bypassed.

nodes.label: Scripts and services

nodes.label: Unregistered API keys
nodes.note: Expensed, shared, and long-lived. Expense data usually finds these months before network analysis does, which makes finance a security telemetry source here.

nodes.label: Discovery
nodes.note: Correlating network telemetry, browser inventory, identity logs and expense records. Four signals in four systems, and no one of them sees all three paths.

nodes.label: AI service inventory
nodes.note: What discovery found, triaged into sanction, replace or block. The artifact that turns a scan result into a programme.

nodes.label: Sanctioned alternative
nodes.note: A supported tenant of the same class of tool. Drawn as a control because it is one: blocking without it relocates the traffic rather than stopping it.

nodes.label: Detection and response
nodes.note: What happens when discovery finds something already carrying regulated data. The part that is an incident rather than a policy conversation.

control.note: An unmanaged or personal device carries the same traffic with none of this, which is why discovery cannot rely on the endpoint alone.
control.title: Device posture and inspection

control.note: One click, all sites, permanent. The broadest standing grant in this catalogue and the least deliberated.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: No enrolment, no approval, and no notification on update. The extension that is reviewed is not necessarily the extension that runs next week.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: Authenticated to the provider and anonymous to the organisation. No contract governs what happens to anything sent here.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Server to server, no browser, no user identity. Invisible to every browser control on this diagram and often the largest volume of the three paths.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: Sees destinations for all three paths, and content only where inspection terminates.
control.title: Independent discovery

control.note: The only signal that finds an extension reading pages it was never invoked on, because that traffic looks like the page load it is attached to.
control.title: Independent discovery

control.note: The signal that finds the direct-API path, and it lives in a system no security team owns. Worth arranging access to before it is needed.
control.title: Independent discovery

edges.label: makes the sanctioned path the easy one

control.note: The only durable outcome. Enforcement without a supported alternative relocates the traffic to something that is harder to find than what was blocked.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: Applied where discovery finds regulated data already in transit. A blunt instrument, and the right one at that point.
control.title: Egress allowlist

crossCutting.note: This archetype is that risk drawn as an architecture. Every node exists because the risk materialised somewhere, and the governance column exists because nothing else will find it.
Three paths, three different detection signals, three different owners. Covering one and declaring the problem solved is the most common failure here.
Extensions and unvetted services are third-party code and third-party processing with no assurance behind either, because no relationship was ever formed to hang assurance on.

deviations.subject: This is drawn as an architecture although nobody designed it
deviations.reason: Every other archetype in the catalogue describes an intended system. This one describes what is found. It is included because the discovered environment is the one the controls have to work in, and because leaving it out would let the catalogue imply that all AI use in an organisation was chosen.

deviations.subject: The governance column carries most of the nodes
deviations.reason: Inverted from every other diagram here, and correct: there is no configuration to harden and no vendor to negotiate with, so discovery and triage are not a plane beside the architecture, they are the architecture.

deviations.subject: A sanctioned alternative is drawn as a control node
deviations.reason: It is a procurement decision rather than a security product, so it does not obviously belong on a security diagram. It is drawn because the evidence is consistent that enforcement without it relocates traffic instead of reducing it, which makes it load-bearing for every other control on the diagram.

archetypes.title: Tenant-wide assistant over your corpus
summary: A vendor-operated assistant granted standing access to the organisation's whole document estate, answering any employee's question by retrieving across it. You configure a tenant; you do not operate an architecture.
description:
Structurally this is retrieval-augmented generation, with one difference that changes every control decision: the retriever, the index, the model and the orchestration are all inside a boundary you cannot inspect. What you own is the identity that authenticates users, the grants that decide what the assistant may read, the permissions already sitting on the source content, the network path, and the contract.
The security question is therefore not "is the vendor's RAG pipeline sound". It is a permissions question you can answer without the vendor's cooperation: given that the assistant inherits a user's entitlements and can search the entire indexed corpus in one turn, what does each user turn out to be entitled to? Over-permissioned content that was safe by obscurity — reachable in principle, never actually found — stops being safe the moment retrieval is exhaustive and instant. This is the dominant failure mode of the archetype and it is a pre-existing condition the assistant surfaces rather than a flaw it introduces.
The second exposure is that indexed content is attacker-writable. Any document a colleague, a customer, or an external collaborator can place into an indexed location is model input for every employee who later asks a related question. Where the assistant can also act — send a message, file a ticket, call a connector — retrieval-borne injection reaches those actions, and the vendor's guardrails are the only thing between the two.
Note what the diagram does not claim. The vendor zone contains its published interfaces and nothing else. Drawing the vendor's retriever, index and orchestrator would be inventing them: those exist, but their configuration, tenancy model and instrumentation are not observable to you, and a diagram that shows them invites controls you cannot actually apply.
distinguishedBy:
Against an embedded retrieval assistant you build: there, the index, the retrieval-time ACL check and the guardrails are yours to design, and the architecture is mostly about getting them right. Here every one of them is the vendor's, and your architecture is the grant model and the edges. Almost no capability transfers between the two.
Against an enterprise AI chat subscription: that archetype connects a general assistant to a handful of sources the user authorises. This one is granted the corpus up front, tenant-wide, by an administrator. The difference is who consents and at what granularity, and it is the difference between a per-user data path and an organisational one.

exemplars.name: Tenant-wide productivity assistants
exemplars.note: Vendor assistants indexing the organisation's mail, files and chat and answering across all of it. Sold as a per-seat add-on to a suite the organisation already runs, which is why the grant decision often precedes any security review.

exemplars.name: Enterprise search assistants
exemplars.note: Standalone vendors that connect to many systems of record and build a unified index. Same shape, more connectors, and the permissions-mirroring question is their central engineering claim — worth testing rather than accepting.

zones.note: Content authored by people outside the organisation that nonetheless lands in indexed locations — inbound mail, shared drives, external collaborators in a workspace.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Where the assistant is actually reached. For a vendor service this is the one place the traffic can still be inspected, which is why endpoint and browser controls carry disproportionate weight on this surface.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: The path between AI System Users and the vendor, and the identity decisions made on it. Operated by the Governance and Platform Provider personas even though nothing behind it is.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: The systems of record the vendor indexes. The permissions here are the real access control — the assistant reflects them, and reflects their mistakes.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: Retrieval, inference, orchestration and logging, none of it observable. Only the published interfaces are drawn.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: What remains enforceable: who may use it, what it may reach, what is visible afterwards, and what the contract obliges the provider to do.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: External content authors
nodes.note: Anyone who can put a document into an indexed location — an inbound email, a shared folder, a guest in a workspace. Their text becomes context for employees who never opened it.

nodes.label: Employee
nodes.note: The assistant answers with this person's entitlements, whatever those turn out to be.

nodes.label: Assistant surface
nodes.note: The in-app panel, browser tab or client the employee types into. The last point at which the prompt and the response are visible to first-party controls.

nodes.label: Browser and DLP controls
nodes.note: Device-resident inspection of what leaves. On a surface where the service cannot be instrumented, this is the substitute for application logging. Note that endpoint detection is absent by construction rather than by oversight: there is no vendor host to install it on, and in-browser inspection is what reaches this traffic instead.

nodes.label: Identity provider
nodes.note: Authenticates the user to the vendor and carries the entitlements the assistant will inherit. Conditional access here is one of the few enforcement points that still binds.

nodes.label: Secure service edge
nodes.note: Inline inspection of traffic to the vendor, and the control that decides which vendor AI services are reachable at all.

nodes.label: Systems of record
nodes.note: Mail, files, chat, tickets, wikis. The authoritative permissions live here, and every over-share predates the assistant.

nodes.label: Indexing grant
nodes.note: The tenant-level authorisation that decides which repositories the vendor may crawl. A single administrative decision that sets the assistant's entire reachable set.

nodes.label: Tenant API
nodes.note: The interface AI System Users and the tenant's connectors talk to. Everything it fronts — retrieval, ranking, inference, orchestration — is the vendor's and is not drawn.

nodes.label: Vendor connectors
nodes.note: The crawl and sync path the vendor runs against the content estate under the indexing grant. Its schedule, retention and permission-mirroring behaviour are the provider's claims, not observations anyone else can make.

nodes.label: Tenant policy
nodes.note: Vendor-side settings the Governance persona configures: who is licensed, which sources are in scope, whether the assistant may act, and what is excluded from indexing.

nodes.label: Exported audit
nodes.note: Whatever the vendor exports, at whatever fidelity and latency it chooses. Plan detection against traffic that is actually visible, not the log the provider may supply.

nodes.label: Vendor assurance
nodes.note: Due diligence, contractual commitments and whatever red-team evidence the vendor will share. On this surface it substitutes for testing that cannot be performed directly.

nodes.label: Shadow AI discovery
nodes.note: Finding the tenants nobody declared. On a surface reached by signing up, the inventory problem precedes every other control.

control.note: Whatever already governs writes to that repository. Nothing AI-specific gates it, and it was designed on the assumption that reaching content required knowing it existed.
control.title: Existing content permissions

control.note: Where TLS inspection is not in place for this vendor, the prompt and response leave uninspected and the endpoint control is the only remaining view.
control.title: Device posture and inspection

control.note: The vendor answers as this user. Everything the assistant will retrieve is decided by the entitlements this assertion carries, so the token is the access-control decision.
control.title: User identity

control.note: Citations are the vendor's claim about its own retrieval. A cited document can be checked for existence and readability by that user; what else was retrieved cannot be checked at all.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: A standing, non-human grant over whole repositories rather than a per-request check. Its scope is the assistant's reachable set, and it is set once by an administrator.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: Not observable. Whether index-time permissions stay in step with the source as content is reshared is the provider's central claim and the central question for assurance.
control.title: Provider-internal

control.note: The Governance persona sets the policy; the provider enforces it. There is no independent way to verify the enforcement, which is precisely what the assurance node exists to compensate for.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: A vendor-shaped view of vendor-side activity. Sufficient for compliance reporting, rarely sufficient for investigation.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: The only control on this edge is legal. Naming it as a control rather than omitting it is the honest treatment of a boundary no technical control reaches.
control.title: Contractual assurance

control.note: Discovery works off traffic and expense data rather than anything the vendor supplies, which is why it finds tenants that were never sanctioned in the first place.
control.title: Independent discovery

crossCutting.note: Not localisable. It is produced jointly by the tenant-wide grant, the pre-existing permissions on the estate, and retrieval that is exhaustive where human search was not. No single node is wrong; the combination is.
Enters through content authored anywhere in the estate and surfaces in any later answer. The injection point and the impact point are different users on different days.
The entire vendor zone is one integrated component you did not build and cannot test. This is what makes third-party assurance a control here rather than a formality.

deviations.subject: The vendor zone shows two interfaces and no internals
deviations.reason: The vendor certainly operates a retriever, an index, a ranker and an inference path. None of it is inspectable, configurable or instrumentable by the customer, so drawing it would suggest control points that do not exist. The two nodes drawn are the interfaces the customer actually integrates with.

deviations.subject: Contractual commitments are drawn as a control edge
deviations.reason: A contract is not a technical control and drawing it as one risks overstating it. It is drawn because omitting it would leave the vendor boundary with no control at all, which understates the position instead. The edge is labelled with its real mechanism so neither reading stands.

deviations.subject: The control plane is marked shared rather than yours
deviations.reason: Policy is authored by the customer and enforced by the provider. Neither owner label alone is true, and CoSAI's shared-responsibility vocabulary has the right word for it.

archetypes.title: Third-party MCP server you consume
summary: A vendor-operated tool server your agents call over the network. You authorise it once, scope it as far as the vendor's OAuth scopes allow, and thereafter it both acts on your systems and writes into your agents' context.
description:
This is a supply-chain relationship with a property ordinary vendor integrations do not have: the vendor supplies text that your model treats as instruction. Tool names, descriptions and results all enter the context window. A hostile or merely careless server needs no vulnerability to influence your agent — describing itself persuasively is sufficient, and descriptions are re-read on each connection rather than fixed at approval time.
What you can verify is narrow and worth stating precisely. You can verify who the server is, at connection time, through OAuth. You can constrain what it may reach, to the granularity of the scopes the vendor chose to publish. You can see what left, if you route agent egress through something that inspects. You cannot verify the server's internal tool catalogue, you cannot put a policy decision point inside its execution, and you cannot test it the way you would test your own code. Those are not gaps in your programme; they are properties of the boundary.
Enterprise-managed authorization changes the shape usefully where it is available. Moving the admission decision to the identity provider — rather than each server's own consent screen — means a security team decides which servers the organisation may connect to, and revocation is one place rather than many. That converts an unbounded set of individually-consented integrations into an administered one, which is the single highest-value change available here.
Accumulation is the quiet risk. Servers are connected for one project, keep their grants, and outlive the reason. Enumerating what is connected and to what scope is the precondition for every other control, and unlike the local tool plane there is at least an identity provider that can answer the question.
distinguishedBy:
Against a remote MCP server you publish: there you are the resource server, you own the tenancy model and the scopes, and the security work is building them properly. Here you are the client, the scopes are someone else's design, and the security work is admission and observation. Almost no capability transfers.
Against the local tool plane: that one is child processes with your privileges and nothing to authenticate to. This one has a real authorization boundary, a revocable grant and an audit trail — a much better position that comes with the loss of any ability to inspect the code.
Against a tenant-wide assistant: that vendor reads your corpus to answer questions. This one acts on your systems on an agent's instruction, and the agent's instruction may have come from content the vendor itself supplied.

exemplars.name: Vendor-published MCP servers
exemplars.note: Major SaaS providers publishing remote tool servers for their own products, so agents can read and write records without a bespoke integration. The mainstream case.

exemplars.name: Aggregator and gateway MCP services
exemplars.note: Third parties fronting many downstream tools behind one server. One grant, many reachable systems, and the scope you approved is not the scope that ultimately gets used.

exemplars.name: Enterprise-managed connection
exemplars.note: Admission moved to the identity provider so a security team, rather than each individual user's consent click, decides which servers may be reached.

zones.note: Other tenants of the same server, and the content that reaches it from elsewhere.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: Wherever the consuming agents run — a workstation or the organisation's own cloud. Drawn as one zone because the relationship with the vendor is the same either way.
zones.label: Compute tier

zones.note: The last place anything can be seen or stopped. On this surface, network position substitutes for instrumentation that does not exist.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: An OAuth resource server run by the Agentic Platform persona. Integration is with its published interface; its catalogue, its execution and its downstream reach are not observable.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Admission, scoping, inventory and assurance — the whole of what the consuming personas actually control here.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Other tenants
nodes.note: Everyone else on the same multi-tenant server. Their isolation is the provider's claim, and it is one of the few things assurance can usefully ask about.

nodes.label: Content the server returns
nodes.note: Records, documents and messages the server reads from systems outside this architecture, passed back as tool results and entering the agent's context as instruction.

nodes.label: Consuming agent
nodes.note: The client. Its authority over the organisation's systems is what the provider's tool results steer.

nodes.label: Tool broker
nodes.note: Where the connection is made and where a description can be pinned, a result can be size- and shape-checked, and a call can be denied. The only insertion point available in this relationship.

nodes.label: Approval gate
nodes.note: For the calls that write. Worth reserving for exactly those, since the read calls are too frequent for a human to remain a real check on them.

nodes.label: Egress inspection
nodes.note: What is going to this vendor and how much of it. The substitute for application logging the provider does not expose.

nodes.label: Vendor MCP server
nodes.note: The published interface. Its tool catalogue is not exposed for verification, and its downstream reach is whatever the vendor built.

nodes.label: Identity provider
nodes.note: Where admission belongs. Deciding centrally which servers may be connected converts a set of individual consent clicks into an administered list with one place to revoke.

nodes.label: Connection inventory
nodes.note: Which servers are connected, by whom, at what scope, and when last used. Grants outlive their projects, and this is the only thing that notices.

nodes.label: Vendor assurance
nodes.note: Tenant isolation, retention, subprocessors, and what happens to the data sent. The questions inspection cannot answer have to be answered by contract.

nodes.label: Call audit
nodes.note: Which tool was called, by which agent, with what arguments. Captured at the broker, because the provider's view of it belongs to the provider.

control.note: The runtime proves what it is on the way out, so the egress path can tell an agent's traffic from anything else leaving the same network.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: Reads skip the approval gate by design — there are too many of them for a human to remain a real check — so this is the first point at which anyone sees them.
control.title: Workload identity

control.note: The strongest authentication in this catalogue: a named client, an explicit scope, and a grant that can be withdrawn in one place. It authenticates the server's identity and says nothing about the honesty of its tool catalogue.
control.title: Delegated grant

control.note: The return path is the risk. Descriptions and results are re-read on every connection and enter the context window as instruction, so what was approved once is not what runs later.
control.title: Authenticated transport

control.note: Not observable. Content the vendor reads from third parties reaches the agent through a connection authorised for something else.
control.title: Provider-internal

control.note: Asserted, not verifiable. This is the specific claim third-party assurance exists to interrogate, because nothing outside the provider can test it.
control.title: Provider-internal

control.note: Moves the decision from an end user's consent screen to a security team's allowlist. The highest-value change available in this archetype.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: A grant not in the registry is not a grant; checking at connect is what makes that true.
control.title: Registry admission

control.note: The only control on the vendor's side of this boundary. Named as a control rather than omitted, and labelled honestly so it is not mistaken for a technical one.
control.title: Contractual assurance

control.note: Captured at the broker rather than requested from the provider, so it exists at the fidelity the consumer needs rather than the one the provider chose.
control.title: Append-only audit

crossCutting.note: Arrives through the return path of a connection you deliberately made. The vendor need not be hostile — it need only relay content from a system that is.
You can verify who the server is and never what its tools do. That asymmetry is the defining property of the archetype and no control on your side closes it.
Grants accumulate across projects and people. Each connection was reasonable; the standing set nobody reviews is not.

deviations.subject: MCP tool security tooling is not listed as a capability here
deviations.reason: It would be the obvious pick and it does not apply. The capability is about verifying a tool catalogue, and a vendor's catalogue is not exposed for verification — the capability taxonomy already records this as structurally unavailable on this surface. What remains is scoping the grant, brokering the call and watching the egress, and those are what is listed.

deviations.subject: Your agent runtime is one zone rather than split by where it runs
deviations.reason: The agent may be on a laptop or in your cloud, and that changes a great deal about the agent and nothing about this relationship. The archetype is the vendor boundary; where the client sits is described by whichever agent archetype applies.

deviations.subject: The vendor zone contains only the server interface
deviations.reason: The vendor certainly runs a tool catalogue, an execution layer and downstream integrations. None is observable, and drawing them would imply controls that do not exist. The interface is what you integrate with and therefore all that is drawn.

archetypes.title: In-app agent acting on vendor records
summary: An agent built into a SaaS product, acting on the records that product holds — resolving tickets, updating opportunities, approving requests. It writes, and the writes are to your system of record.
description:
The distinction from a vendor assistant that answers questions is the write path, and it changes everything downstream. A wrong answer is a wrong answer; a wrong write is a changed record, an email that went out, a refund that was issued. Reversibility, not accuracy, is the property to design for, and it is a property of the vendor's action catalogue rather than of anything you configure.
The attacker is frequently your own authenticated customer. Support and service agents read ticket text, form submissions and uploaded documents — content supplied by whoever opened the case — and act on the tenant's records with the tenant's authority. Injection here does not require a breach; it requires filling in a text field. This is the archetype where indirect prompt injection has the shortest path from untrusted input to consequential action.
Your control surface is the action catalogue and the identity it runs as. Which actions the agent may take, on which record types, under which conditions, and whether a human approves the consequential ones are all vendor-exposed settings — usually generous by default, because the product is sold on autonomy. The agent's own identity, where the vendor gives it one distinct from a service account, is what makes its actions attributable afterwards.
What you cannot do is insert a policy decision point into the vendor's loop. There is no place to put a runtime enforcement layer between the model's decision and the record write. Every control is therefore either upstream of the loop — scoping what it may reach — or downstream of it, in review and reversal.
distinguishedBy:
Against the tenant-wide assistant: that one reads across your corpus and answers. This one acts within one product's data model and writes. The read archetype's central question is permissions; this one's is reversibility.
Against an autonomous action agent you build: identical shape, opposite ownership. There you design the action allowlist, the approval threshold and the compensating transaction. Here you choose from a menu, and what is not on the menu is not available.

exemplars.name: Customer service and support agents
exemplars.note: Vendor agents that resolve tickets end to end — reading the customer's message, searching knowledge, and issuing refunds or account changes without a human in between.

exemplars.name: CRM and ITSM in-app agents
exemplars.note: Agents inside sales and service platforms acting on opportunities, cases and change records under a configurable action catalogue.

exemplars.name: Line-of-business SaaS with bolted-on agents
exemplars.note: Agent features added to products bought for something else. Same architecture, usually a thinner control catalogue and no separate agent identity.

zones.note: The organisation's customers, and the text they put in fields the agent reads.
zones.label: Outside world

zones.note: The humans who supervise, review and reverse — where any of those happen.
zones.label: Endpoint

zones.note: How staff and systems reach the vendor, and who they are asserted to be.
zones.label: Network and identity edge

zones.note: What the vendor's agent reaches beyond the vendor: billing, directory, warehouse. Frequently the real blast radius, and frequently forgotten.
zones.label: Data tier

zones.note: The agent loop, the model and the record store. Configurable by the Governance persona, instrumentable by nobody outside the provider.
zones.label: Provider

zones.note: Configuration the Governance persona authors and the provider enforces, plus what is observable from outside.
zones.label: Control plane

nodes.label: Customer-supplied text
nodes.note: Ticket bodies, form fields, uploaded documents, email replies. Read by the agent as context and, by construction, authored by someone with an interest in the outcome.

nodes.label: Reviewing staff
nodes.note: Approves the actions the vendor permits gating, and reverses the ones nobody gated. The threshold between those two is the archetype's central configuration decision.

nodes.label: Admin console
nodes.note: Where the action catalogue, the thresholds and the agent's permissions are set.

nodes.label: Identity provider
nodes.note: Authenticates staff and, where the vendor supports it, issues the agent an identity of its own rather than letting it act as a shared service account.

nodes.label: Network inspection
nodes.note: What is being sent to the vendor, and what the vendor's callbacks bring back.

nodes.label: Downstream systems of record
nodes.note: Billing, entitlements, directory. Reached through integrations the vendor's agent can invoke, and the point at which a wrong action stops being reversible by editing a record.

nodes.label: Vendor agent platform
nodes.note: Where the loop runs. No policy decision point can be inserted into it — the capability taxonomy records that as structurally unavailable on this surface, and it is the reason every control here sits upstream or downstream of the loop.

nodes.label: Vendor integrations
nodes.note: How the agent reaches beyond the vendor's own data model into the organisation's systems. Authorised once, per integration, and usually more broadly than any single action requires.

nodes.label: Action catalogue and thresholds
nodes.note: Which actions the agent may take, on what, and where a human is required. Generous by default, because autonomy is what the product is sold on.

nodes.label: Agent identity
nodes.note: A distinct, revocable principal for the agent rather than a shared service account. Without it, no action it takes is attributable and no single action can be revoked.

nodes.label: Outcome monitoring
nodes.note: Watching what the agent actually did — refund rates, escalation rates, records touched. Behavioural monitoring substitutes for runtime enforcement that cannot be installed here.

nodes.label: Disable control
nodes.note: Turning the agent off without a vendor support ticket. Worth confirming it exists before it is needed, because on this surface it is a product feature rather than something the consumer can build.

control.note: The vendor's guardrail on case text. Configurable and not verifiable, which is why the action catalogue and the reversal path are the controls that actually bound this.
control.title: Content inspection

control.note: Administering the agent is administering everything it may do, so this session deserves the same treatment as any other privileged access path.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: The same channel configures the agent and reviews it. Privileged access to this console is privileged access to the agent's entire permission set.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: Only fires for actions the catalogue marks as gated. Everything else has already happened by the time anyone sees it.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: Not observable. The decision to act and the act itself are both inside the boundary.
control.title: Provider-internal

control.note: A service principal the organisation issued, scoped per integration rather than per action. The agent inherits everything that credential can do, not just what this action needed.
control.title: Brokered credential

control.note: First-party records of what changed. Often the only trustworthy account of what the agent did, because it is the one the provider does not write.
control.title: Append-only audit

control.note: The Governance persona authors it, the provider enforces it, and neither can verify the other. This is the canonical shared-responsibility edge on this surface.
control.title: Tenant configuration

control.note: Where the vendor supports it. Where it does not, the agent shares a service account with every other integration and nothing it does is separately attributable or revocable.
control.title: Agent identity

control.note: Measured outside the provider boundary, which is what makes it reliable. The vendor's view of its own agent's behaviour is the vendor's.
control.title: Independent discovery

control.note: Depends entirely on the vendor having built it. Test it during evaluation rather than during an incident.
control.title: Tenant configuration

crossCutting.note: Untrusted input, an unobservable loop, and a write path into systems of record. No node owns this — it is what the archetype is, and the controls are all upstream scoping or downstream reversal because the middle is not yours.
The agent acts through integration credentials you issued for a system, not for a decision. Its authority is the union of every integration, and no single action narrows it.
The connector grants set the reach, the action catalogue sets the intent, and neither is scoped by the other.

deviations.subject: Your downstream systems are drawn as a zone you own, inside a SaaS archetype
deviations.reason: They are not part of the vendor's architecture, and a diagram of the vendor's agent would stop at its boundary. They are drawn because the write path into them is where this archetype becomes consequential, and omitting them would make the blast radius look like one product's record store.

deviations.subject: The agent's own decision loop is not drawn
deviations.reason: It exists and it is the most interesting part. It is also entirely unobservable and unconfigurable, and the capability taxonomy already records that no runtime enforcement can be inserted into it. Drawing a loop nobody can reach would invite controls that do not exist.

deviations.subject: A disable control is drawn as a governance node
deviations.reason: On a surface you operate, a kill switch is something you build. Here it is a checkbox the vendor either shipped or did not, so it is drawn as a control-plane node whose note says to verify it exists before relying on it.
